If Sturdimade has sold ten million cars worldwide, a few hundred survivors tells us almost nothing about the odds for the car you're about to buy.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer that says the evidence comes from a biased sample: cases chosen precisely because they already show the thing the conclusion wants to prove. It might also be phrased as \"fails to consider how many Sturdimades did not last.\"\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\nThis is the biased sample flaw, described abstractly. Translate it back into the argument:\n- \"draws a general conclusion\": *any* Sturdimade you buy will last.\n- \"from cases selected only on the basis of having a characteristic that favors that conclusion\": the club members, who were selected for having driven 100,000+ miles.\n\nAny time the sample is filtered by the very trait you're trying to prove, the sample can't prove it. It's like surveying people at a marathon finish line and concluding that everyone who starts a marathon finishes it.\n\n**(B) Circular Reasoning.**\nA circular argument's evidence just repeats the conclusion. Here the evidence is about a few hundred club members, and the conclusion is about any Sturdimade a new buyer might purchase. Those are different claims. The problem is that the evidence is weak, not that it's the same as the conclusion.\n\n**(C) Equivocation.**\nFor this to be the flaw, a key term would need to shift meaning between the premises and the conclusion. The only candidate is \"long distance,\" and it means the same thing throughout: lots of miles. No term is doing double duty.\n\n**(D) Not an Objection.**\nDoes anything in the evidence cut against the conclusion? Cars driving 300,000 miles is, if anything, what the advertiser *wants* you to hear. The evidence is weak support, not contrary support.\n\n**(E) Wrong Flaw.**\nThis is the tempting one for students who latch onto the word \"popular\" in the first sentence. But \"popular\" only describes which group of cars Sturdimade belongs to. The argument never says \"people love Sturdimades, so they must last.\" Its evidence is mileage, not opinion.\n\n---\n\n## 2. PT114-S1-Q23 · Flaw · Difficulty 3 · Answer A\n\n> Activist: Food producers irradiate food in order to prolong its shelf life. Five animal studies were recently conducted to investigate whether this process alters food in a way that could be dangerous to people who eat it. The studies concluded that irradiated food is safe for humans to eat. However, because these studies were subsequently found by a panel of independent scientists to be seriously flawed in their methodology, it follows that irradiated food is not safe for human consumption.\n>\n> The reasoning in the activist's argument is flawed because that argument\n>\n> (A) treats a failure to prove a claim as constituting proof of the denial of that claim · (B) treats methodological flaws in past studies as proof that it is currently not possible to devise methodologically adequate alternatives · (C) fails to consider the possibility that even a study whose methodology has no serious flaws nonetheless might provide only weak support for its conclusion · (D) fails to consider the possibility that what is safe for animals might not always be safe for human beings · (E) fails to establish that the independent scientists know more about food irradiation than do the people who produced the five studies\n\nA 72% · B 11% · C 7% · D 2% · E 8%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (it follows that)**\nIrradiated food is not safe for human consumption.\n\n**Evidence**\nFive animal studies concluded irradiated food is safe for humans. An independent panel later found those studies seriously flawed in their methodology.\n\n**Evaluate**\nLet's be generous and grant everything the activist says. The studies were badly designed. The panel is right.\n\nWhat does that get us? It means we can't trust the studies' conclusion that irradiated food is *safe*. So now we don't know whether it's safe.\n\nBut \"we don't know it's safe\" is a long way from \"it's not safe.\" Knocking out the evidence for a claim leaves you with no evidence either way. It doesn't hand you evidence for the opposite.\n\n*Given that ...* the only studies saying irradiated food is safe are worthless,\n  *How could we argue that ...* irradiated food is still safe?\n  Easy. Maybe it just is safe, and those five studies happened to be sloppy ways of showing something true. A bad argument for a true claim is still a true claim.\n\n**Goal**\nThis is the famous flaw of treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence. Look for an answer saying the author took \"this wasn't proven\" as proof of \"the opposite is true.\"\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\nLine it up with the argument:\n- \"a failure to prove a claim\": the flawed studies failed to prove that irradiated food is safe.\n- \"as constituting proof of the denial of that claim\": the activist concludes irradiated food is *not* safe.\n\nWhen the evidence for a claim collapses, the right conclusion is \"we don't know,\" not \"the claim is false.\" Whenever an argument goes from \"their evidence is bad\" to \"their conclusion is wrong,\" check for this flaw first.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nThe activist says nothing about whether better studies could be designed now. For all she cares, someone could run a perfect study tomorrow. Her conclusion is about whether irradiated food is safe, not about whether it's possible to study it properly.\n\n**(C) Not an Objection.**\n\"Fails to consider\" means we can ask whether this idea would weaken the argument. It wouldn't. The point is that even good studies can give weak support. That only makes the five studies' conclusion *less* trustworthy, which is the activist's side of the fight. You can't criticize an argument by handing it more ammunition.\n\n**(D) Not an Objection.**\nSame test: would this weaken the activist? No. \"What's safe for animals might not be safe for humans\" is another reason to doubt the animal studies. The activist is the one attacking those studies, so this helps her. It would be a good objection to the *studies'* conclusion, not to hers.\n\n**(E) Not an Objection.**\nThis is the most tempting wrong answer for students who want to attack the panel. But go back to the Evaluate step: we already granted that the panel is completely right and the studies are completely flawed, and the argument *still* doesn't work. So questioning the panel's expertise can't be the core problem. Even with perfect experts, \"the studies are bad\" doesn't prove \"the food is unsafe.\"\n\n---\n\n## 3. PT159-S1-Q21 · Flaw · Difficulty 5 · Answer D\n\n> Professor O'Brien: Any of my students who heard Mercado's lecture from the beginning would have thought it was fascinating, and I know that some of my students did think it was fascinating, so some of my students must have heard it from the beginning.\n>\n> Professor O'Brien's argument does not follow logically from its premises because of the possibility that\n>\n> (A) some of Professor O'Brien's students are very interested in Mercado's work but were unable to attend the lecture · (B) many people who are not Professor O'Brien's students did not think that the lecture was fascinating, even though they heard it from the beginning · (C) some of Professor O'Brien's students were a few minutes late for the lecture and did not find the lecture fascinating · (D) no one who heard the lecture from the beginning and thought that it was fascinating was one of Professor O'Brien's students · (E) not everyone who arrived at the lecture on time was able to hear the entire lecture because of disruptions caused by those who were late in arriving\n\nA 14% · B 10% · C 6% · D 57% · E 13%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (so)**\nSome of O'Brien's students must have heard the lecture from the beginning.\n\n**Evidence**\n- If one of O'Brien's students heard it from the beginning, then that student found it fascinating.\n  *O'Brien student + heard from beginning → fascinating*\n- Some of O'Brien's students found it fascinating.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThe rule tells us what happens when a student heard the lecture from the beginning: they find it fascinating. It doesn't tell us that being fascinated means they heard it from the beginning.\n\nO'Brien has the rule running backward. She sees the outcome (fascinated students) and concludes the trigger (heard from the beginning) must have happened.\n\nThink of it this way: \"Anyone who eats a whole pizza is full. Some of my students are full. So some of my students ate a whole pizza.\" Maybe they ate a salad. Being full has other causes.\n\nSame here. A student could walk in twenty minutes late and still think it was the best lecture of their life. The rule never says the late students can't be fascinated.\n\n**Goal**\nThe stem asks for a *possibility* that shows the conclusion doesn't follow. That means we want a scenario where both premises stay true and the conclusion turns out false.\n\nThe conclusion is false if *none* of O'Brien's students heard it from the beginning. So picture this: every one of her fascinated students came in late. The rule is untouched (no student heard it from the beginning, so the rule never triggers), some students found it fascinating, and zero students heard it from the start.\n\nLook for an answer that describes that world: no O'Brien student heard it from the beginning, or the fascinated ones didn't.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Doesn't Break the Conclusion.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer. It tells us about students who weren't there at all. Fine. But the conclusion only needs *some* students to have heard it from the beginning. Students who stayed home say nothing about the ones who came. Even with (A) true, the fascinated students could still be early arrivals, and the conclusion could still be true.\n\nOn \"does not follow because of the possibility that\" questions, the right answer has to put pressure on the conclusion itself. Ask of each answer: if this were true, would O'Brien's conclusion be in trouble? Here, no.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nThe rule is only about O'Brien's students. What people outside her class thought has no bearing on either premise or on the conclusion. (And non-students hearing it from the start would, if anything, show the lecture was well attended from the beginning, which doesn't hurt O'Brien.)\n\n**(C) Doesn't Break the Conclusion.**\nLate students who weren't fascinated fit perfectly well into O'Brien's world. They don't trigger the rule (they didn't hear it from the beginning), and they aren't the fascinated students she's talking about. Her conclusion is about the fascinated ones. (C) would need to say the late students *were* fascinated to do any damage.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nRead it carefully, because it's built to look convoluted: nobody who both heard it from the beginning *and* found it fascinating was one of O'Brien's students.\n\nNow bring in the rule: any O'Brien student who heard it from the beginning *would* have found it fascinating. So if an O'Brien student had heard it from the beginning, that student would be exactly the kind of person (D) says doesn't exist. The only way (D) and the rule can both be true is if no O'Brien student heard it from the beginning.\n\nThat's the conclusion, flatly false, with both premises still standing. The fascinated students must have gotten there late. This is the scenario we predicted.\n\n**(E) Doesn't Break the Conclusion.**\nDisruptions affected who heard the *entire* lecture, but the argument is about who heard it from the *beginning*. Someone who arrived on time and got distracted by latecomers still heard the start. (E) doesn't stop any O'Brien student from hearing the beginning, so the conclusion survives.\n\n---\n\n## 4. PT104-S4-Q23 · Most Supported · Difficulty 2 · Answer E\n\n> Much of today's literature is inferior: most of our authors are intellectually and emotionally inexperienced, and their works lack both the intricacy and the focus on the significant that characterize good literature. However, Hypatia's latest novel is promising; it shows a maturity, complexity, and grace that far exceeds that of her earlier works.\n>\n> Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?\n>\n> (A) Much of today's literature focuses less on the significant than Hypatia's latest novel focuses on the significant. · (B) Much of today's literature at least lacks the property of grace. · (C) Hypatia's latest novel is good literature when judged by today's standards. · (D) Hypatia's latest novel is clearly better than the majority of today's literature. · (E) Hypatia's latest novel has at least one property of good literature to a greater degree than her earlier works.\n\nA 6% · B 2% · C 4% · D 4% · E 84%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements**\n- Much of today's literature is inferior.\n- Most authors today are intellectually and emotionally inexperienced.\n- Their works lack intricacy and a focus on the significant, which are what characterize good literature.\n- Hypatia's latest novel is promising. It shows maturity, complexity and grace far beyond her *earlier works*.\n\n**Evaluate**\nNotice what Hypatia's novel is being compared to. Not today's literature. Her own earlier books.\n\nThat matters, because the tempting inferences will try to rank her novel against everyone else's. We can't do that. We know her new book beats her old books. We don't know how it stacks up against anyone else.\n\nNow look for a bridge between the two halves. Good literature has *intricacy* and *a focus on the significant*. Hypatia's new novel shows more *complexity*. Intricacy and complexity are close enough to be the same property. So her new novel has more of one of the things good literature has.\n\nAlso notice the word \"promising.\" That's the author being careful. Promising isn't the same as good.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for a modest answer: Hypatia's latest novel shows more of a good-literature trait (complexity/intricacy) than her earlier work did. Be suspicious of anything that compares her to other authors or calls her novel good literature.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported Comparison.**\nWe have no idea whether Hypatia's new novel focuses on the significant at all. The passage lists maturity, complexity and grace. \"Focus on the significant\" isn't on that list. So we can't say her novel beats anyone on that score.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.**\nThe passage says today's works lack intricacy and focus on the significant. Grace shows up only in the description of Hypatia's novel. Nothing tells us the rest of today's literature lacks grace.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.**\n\"Promising\" is not \"good.\" The author is holding back on purpose. All we know is that the new book is better than Hypatia's earlier books. If her earlier books were terrible, \"much better than terrible\" could still fall short of good literature.\n\n**(D) Unsupported Comparison.**\nTwo problems. First, the only comparison in the passage is to her *earlier* works, not to today's literature. Second, \"much\" of today's literature is inferior, which isn't the same as \"the majority.\" Even if we knew she beat the inferior stuff, we couldn't say that's most of it.\n\n**(E) Correct.**\nIt stays inside the one comparison we actually have (new novel vs. her earlier works) and only claims *at least one* property. Complexity is that property: it matches the intricacy that characterizes good literature, and her new novel has more of it than her old ones.\n\nOn Most Supported questions, \"at least one\" and similar modest wording is a good sign. The right answer usually claims just enough to be backed by the passage and not a word more.\n\n---\n\n## 5. PT109-S3-Q3 · Paradox EXCEPT · Difficulty 1 · Answer B\n\n> The most common bird in Stillwater Marsh is a species of marsh hen, yet this species is rarely seen, even by experienced bird-watchers who seek it. In fact, this bird is seen far less frequently than any other bird inhabiting the marsh, including those that are much smaller and much less abundant.\n>\n> Each of the following, if true, helps to reconcile the statements above except:\n>\n> (A) The coloration of the marsh hen blends in particularly well with the marsh grass where the marsh hen nests. · (B) The marsh hen's call is harsh and repetitive, whereas the calls of many other marsh birds are pleasant and melodious. · (C) Unlike many small marsh birds, which dash along the banks of the marsh, the marsh hen remains completely still for long periods of time. · (D) Many marsh birds are most active during daylight hours, but the marsh hen is usually most active at night. · (E) Although many small marsh birds fly in groups to several feeding areas each day, the marsh hen tends to be solitary and flies only when it is in danger.\n\nA 3% · B 92% · C 2% · D 2% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that ...**\nThe marsh hen is the most common bird in Stillwater Marsh.\n\n**How can it be that ...**\nIt's seen less often than any other bird in the marsh, even smaller and rarer ones, and even by experienced bird-watchers looking for it?\n\n**Evaluate**\nWe'd expect the most common bird to be the one people see most. So something about the marsh hen must make it hard to *see*, no matter how many of them there are.\n\nWhat makes a bird hard to spot?\n- It blends in.\n- It doesn't move much.\n- It's out when people aren't (night).\n- It stays hidden and rarely flies.\n\n**Goal**\nFour answers will give the marsh hen some reason to be hard to see. The odd one out will either have nothing to do with being seen, or it will make the hen *easier* to notice.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Helps Explain.**\nCamouflage. If the hen blends into the grass where it nests, you can walk right past a hundred of them and never see one.\n\n**(B) Correct.**\nA call is something you *hear*, not see. And a harsh, repetitive call is, if anything, going to help a bird-watcher find the hen, not hide it from them. This doesn't explain why such a common bird is so rarely seen, so it's the exception.\n\nWhen an EXCEPT answer talks about a different sense or a different kind of evidence than the paradox is about (hearing vs. seeing), it's usually the one that doesn't help.\n\n**(C) Helps Explain.**\nMovement catches the eye. The small birds are dashing around on the banks; the marsh hen sits frozen for long stretches. Still birds are much harder to spot.\n\n**(D) Helps Explain.**\nIf the marsh hen does its business at night, while bird-watchers are out during the day, of course it gets seen less.\n\n**(E) Helps Explain.**\nBirds flying in flocks to feeding areas are easy to spot. A bird that stays alone and only flies when it's in danger mostly stays hidden in the grass.\n\n---\n\n## 6. PT108-S3-Q6 · Paradox EXCEPT · Difficulty 4 · Answer C\n\n*Breakdown only. This question already has LSAT Lab's five Choice Notes, which stay as they are.*\n\n> Shortly after the power plant opened and began discharging its wastewater into the river, there was a decrease in the overall number of bass caught by anglers downstream from the plant.\n>\n> Each of the following, if true, could explain the decrease described above EXCEPT:\n>\n> (A) The discharged wastewater made the river more attractive to fish that are the natural predators of bass. · (B) The discharged water was warmer than the normal river temperature, leading the bass to seek cooler water elsewhere. · (C) Because of the new plant, access to the part of the river downstream from the plant was improved, leading to an increase in the number of anglers fishing for bass. · (D) Because of the new plant, the level of noise downstream increased, making that section of the river a less popular place for anglers to fish. · (E) The discharged wastewater created turbulence that disrupted the vegetation of the river downstream, destroying some of the bass's natural habitat.\n\nA 1% · B 1% · C 65% · D 30% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that ...**\nThe power plant opened and started dumping wastewater into the river.\n\n**Why is it that ...**\nShortly after, anglers downstream caught fewer bass overall?\n\n**Evaluate**\nThis isn't a true paradox. Nothing here is surprising. The stem just wants explanations for a drop in the number of bass caught.\n\nThink about what \"number of bass caught\" depends on. It takes two things: bass in the water and people fishing for them. So there are two roads to fewer bass caught:\n1. **Fewer bass downstream.** They died, got eaten, moved away, or lost their habitat.\n2. **Less fishing downstream.** Fewer anglers, or anglers fishing less.\n\nStudents tend to only think of road 1, because the wastewater feels like it must be hurting the fish. But road 2 is just as good. If half the anglers stop showing up, half as many bass get caught, even if the bass are doing great.\n\n**Goal**\nExpect four answers that take one of those two roads: fewer bass, or fewer people fishing. The exception will do neither, or it will push the other way (more bass or more fishing, which should mean *more* bass caught).\n\nBe careful with any answer about anglers. It isn't out of scope. Anglers are half the equation.\n\n---\n\n## 7. PT156-S4-Q10 · Paradox EXCEPT · Difficulty 5 · Answer D\n\n*Not loaded yet. The bank labels this Most Strongly Supported; it's a Paradox EXCEPT.*\n\n> While the population of city X is approximately one-half that of city Y, the number of city X residents who are patients in hospitals is only one-fourth that of the number of city Y residents who are patients in hospitals.\n>\n> Each of the following, if true, contributes to an explanation of the difference in the number of residents who are patients in hospitals except:\n>\n> (A) Preventive health programs are more prevalent in city X than in city Y. · (B) The hospitals in city X are noted as leaders in employing outpatient treatment wherever possible. · (C) The drinking water of city Y has dangerously high levels of pollutants, whereas this is not the case for city X. · (D) The hospitals in city Y are of very high quality, and residents of city X are often sent there for treatment. · (E) The lifestyle in city X is significantly less stressful than the lifestyle in city Y.\n\nA 3% · B 14% · C 4% · D 61% · E 18%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that ...**\nCity X has about half the population of city Y.\n\n**How can it be that ...**\nCity X has only a quarter as many residents in the hospital?\n\n**Evaluate**\nPut numbers on it. Say city X has 100,000 people and city Y has 200,000. If X has 100 residents in the hospital, Y has 400.\n\nThat's 1 in 1,000 for X and 2 in 1,000 for Y. Per person, X residents end up in the hospital half as often.\n\nSo we need reasons that a resident of city X is less likely to be a hospital patient. Two roads:\n1. **X residents are healthier.** Less disease, less pollution, better prevention, less stress.\n2. **Sick X residents are less likely to be *admitted*.** They get treated some other way, so they never count as \"patients in hospitals.\"\n\nNow the key detail, the one the whole question turns on: the stat counts *residents* of each city who are patients in hospitals. It doesn't say which city's hospitals. An X resident in a hospital in city Y is still an X resident who's a hospital patient.\n\n**Goal**\nFour answers will give X residents a reason to be healthier or less likely to be admitted. The exception will explain something else, most likely which *hospitals* are busy, rather than which city's *residents* are in them.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Contributes to an Explanation.**\nPreventive programs mean fewer people get sick enough to need a hospital. That's road 1: X residents are healthier.\n\n**(B) Contributes to an Explanation.**\nOutpatient treatment means you get treated and go home the same day. You're never admitted, so you're never counted as a patient in the hospital. X's sick residents are getting care without landing in a hospital bed. That's road 2.\n\nThis is the tempting one because it sounds like good news about X's hospitals rather than an explanation. But remember what we're counting: residents *who are patients in hospitals*. Outpatient care keeps people out of that count.\n\n**(C) Contributes to an Explanation.**\nPolluted drinking water in Y makes Y residents sick more often. More sick Y residents, more Y residents in the hospital. The paradox is about the *ratio* between the two cities, so a reason Y is worse off works just as well as a reason X is better off.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nThis tells us X residents often get sent to Y's hospitals. But where they're treated doesn't change who they are. An X resident in a Y hospital is still counted as an X resident who is a patient in a hospital.\n\nSo (D) explains why Y's *hospitals* might be crowded. It does nothing to explain why fewer *X residents* are hospital patients. If anything, being sent for treatment points to X residents *being* hospitalized, which is the opposite of what we need.\n\nHard EXCEPT questions often hinge on one precise word in the stimulus. Here it was \"residents.\" When you get stuck between answers, go back and ask what exactly is being counted.\n\n**(E) Contributes to an Explanation.**\nThis was the most popular wrong answer, probably because stress feels like a weak or indirect reason. But the stem only asks what \"contributes to an explanation,\" which is a low bar. Less stress means fewer stress-related illnesses (heart problems, for example), which means fewer X residents in the hospital. It doesn't have to explain the whole gap. It just has to help.\n\n---\n\n## 8. PT110-S2-Q8 · Method · Difficulty 2 · Answer A\n\n> Conservationist: The risk to airplane passengers from collisions between airplanes using the airport and birds from the wildlife refuge is negligible. In the 10 years since the refuge was established, only 20 planes have been damaged in collisions with birds, and no passenger has been injured as a result of such a collision. The wildlife refuge therefore poses no safety risk.\n>\n> Pilot: You neglect to mention that 17 of those 20 collisions occurred within the past 2 years, and that the number of birds in the refuge is rapidly increasing. As the number of collisions between birds and airplanes increases, so does the likelihood that at least one such collision will result in passenger injuries.\n>\n> The pilot counters the conservationist by\n>\n> (A) attempting to show that the conservationist's description of the facts is misleading · (B) questioning the conservationist's motives for reaching a certain conclusion · (C) asserting that dangerous situations inevitably become more dangerous with the passage of time · (D) discrediting the moral principle on which the conservationist's argument is based · (E) disputing the accuracy of the figures cited by the conservationist\n\nA 85% · B 0% · C 10% · D 0% · E 5%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conservationist's Conclusion (therefore)**\nThe wildlife refuge poses no safety risk to airplane passengers.\n\n**Conservationist's Evidence**\nIn 10 years, only 20 planes have been damaged by birds from the refuge, and no passengers have been hurt.\n\n**Pilot's Response**\n17 of those 20 collisions happened in just the last 2 years, and the bird population is growing fast. More collisions means a higher chance one of them hurts a passenger.\n\n**Evaluate**\nNotice what the pilot does *not* say. He doesn't say \"it wasn't 20 collisions\" or \"actually someone was injured.\" He accepts the conservationist's numbers.\n\nWhat he attacks is the picture those numbers paint. \"20 collisions in 10 years\" sounds like 2 a year, steady and harmless. But most of them happened recently, so the real rate is climbing fast. The 10-year average hides a trend.\n\nThis is the most common move a second speaker makes on the LSAT. They almost never deny the first speaker's evidence. They add a fact that changes what the evidence means.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer that says the pilot accepts the facts but argues they were presented in a way that gives the wrong impression.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\n\"Misleading\" is the right word. The conservationist's facts are accurate, but her description (20 over 10 years, no injuries) leaves out the timing that makes them look safe. The pilot fills in the missing piece to show the real risk is growing.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nThe pilot never suggests the conservationist has a hidden agenda. He doesn't say \"you just want to protect the birds.\" He argues with her reasoning, not her motives.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.**\nThis is the trap for students who notice the pilot is talking about the future. But the pilot's point is specific: collisions are rising *because* the birds are increasing, and more collisions raise the risk. He never says dangerous situations *inevitably* get worse just because time passes. Time isn't the cause in his argument. More birds is.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.**\nThere's no moral principle anywhere in the conservationist's argument. It's about safety risk, which is a factual question. There's nothing for the pilot to discredit.\n\n**(E) Bad Description.**\nThe pilot doesn't dispute the figures. He uses them. \"17 of *those* 20 collisions\" only works if the 20 is accurate. This is exactly the move the second speaker almost never makes.\n\n---\n\n## 9. PT117-S3-Q8 · Method · Difficulty 3 · Answer A\n\n*Choice Notes only. This question already has an Argument Breakdown, which stays as it is. The bank labels it Weaken; the stem asks how Rossi's argument proceeds, so it's Method.*\n\n> Rossi: It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented. So children should have the right to vote, since sometimes the interests of children are different from those of their parents.\n>\n> Smith: Granted, children's interests are not always the same as their parents'; governmental deficits incurred by their parents' generation will later affect their own generation's standard of living. But even if children are told about the issues affecting them, which is not generally the case, their conceptions of what can or should be done are too simple, and their time horizons are radically different from those of adults, so we cannot give them the responsibility of voting.\n>\n> Which one of the following most accurately describes Rossi's argument?\n>\n> (A) It makes an appeal to a general principle. · (B) It denies the good faith of an opponent. · (C) It relies on evaluating the predictable consequences of a proposal. · (D) It substitutes description for giving a rationale for a policy. · (E) It employs a term on two different occasions in different senses.\n\nA 78% · B 1% · C 6% · D 11% · E 4%\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\nRossi's first sentence is a general rule: it's undemocratic for *anyone* to live under a government that doesn't represent their interests. Then he applies it to one group. Children's interests sometimes differ from their parents', so (by the rule) children need their own representation, which means the vote.\n\n\"Appeal to a general principle\" is how the LSAT describes this. Anytime an argument opens with a broad \"it is wrong / undemocratic / unfair to ...\" and then applies it to a specific case, this answer is in play.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.**\nRossi speaks first. He has no opponent yet, and he never questions anyone's honesty or intentions. Smith doesn't do this either, for what it's worth.\n\n**(C) Bad Description.**\nRossi's argument is about what's *democratic*, not about what would happen if children voted. He never predicts any results of giving children the vote. If anyone looks at practical consequences, it's Smith, who worries children's views are too simple for the responsibility. That's a reason this answer might feel familiar: it's in the neighborhood of the other speaker.\n\n**(D) Bad Description.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer, maybe because Rossi's argument is short and feels like it's just stating things. But he does give a rationale. The policy is \"children should vote.\" The rationale is the principle (unrepresented interests are undemocratic) plus the fact (children's interests sometimes differ). That's a reason, not just a description.\n\n**(E) Bad Description.**\nThis describes equivocation. The only term Rossi uses twice is \"interests,\" and it means the same thing both times: what's good for a person. No shift in meaning.\n\n---\n\n## 10. PT112-S1-Q3 · Necessary Assumption · Difficulty 3 · Answer C\n\n> Finnish author Jaakko Mikkeli was accused by Norwegian author Kirsten Halden of plagiarizing a book that she had written and that had been published 20 years before Mikkeli's. The two books, although set in different periods and regions, contain enough plot similarities to make coincidental resemblance unlikely. Mikkeli's defense rests on his argument that plagiarism was impossible in this case because Halden's book has been published only in Norwegian, a language Mikkeli does not understand, and because no reviews of Halden's book have ever been published.\n>\n> The argument in Mikkeli's defense depends on the assumption that\n>\n> (A) Mikkeli has never met Halden · (B) Halden's book did not become popular in Norway · (C) nobody related the plot of Halden's book in detail to Mikkeli before Mikkeli wrote his book · (D) there is a common European myth to which both authors referred subconsciously in the books in question · (E) Mikkeli is not familiar with Old Icelandic, an extinct language related to an earlier form of Norwegian\n\nA 1% · B 6% · C 80% · D 1% · E 12%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nIt was impossible for Mikkeli to plagiarize Halden's book.\n\n**Evidence**\n- Halden's book has only been published in Norwegian, and Mikkeli can't read Norwegian.\n- No reviews of Halden's book were ever published.\n\n**Evaluate**\nMikkeli's defense is: I had no way to learn what's in that book. He's closed two doors. He couldn't read it himself, and he couldn't read a review summarizing it.\n\n*Given that ...* he can't read Norwegian and there are no reviews,\n  *How could we argue that ...* he still could have plagiarized it?\n\nWhat other doors are there?\n- Someone who reads Norwegian could have told him the plot.\n- An unpublished translation could have been passed around.\n- There could have been a movie, a radio adaptation, or a talk about the book.\n\n\"Impossible\" is a strong word. To claim plagiarism was impossible, Mikkeli needs every door closed, not just the two he mentions.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for a defender: an answer that shuts one of the other doors, most likely \"no one told Mikkeli the plot.\" Negate the correct answer and it should hand us a route for Mikkeli to have learned the story.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not Necessary.**\nNegate it: Mikkeli *has* met Halden. So what? Meeting her doesn't mean she told him the plot of her book. (If she had, that's the scenario in (C).) Shaking someone's hand at a conference doesn't make plagiarism possible.\n\n**(B) Not Necessary.**\nNegate it: Halden's book *was* popular in Norway. That doesn't give Mikkeli a way in. Lots of Norwegians reading it doesn't mean any of them passed the story to a Finnish author who can't read Norwegian. Popularity might make it *more likely* someone talked about it, but that's the idea in (C), not this one.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\nNegate it: someone *did* tell Mikkeli the plot of Halden's book in detail before he wrote his. Now plagiarism is very possible. He didn't need to read Norwegian or find a review. He just needed a friend who'd read it.\n\nThis is a defender. It protects the argument from an objection rather than linking the evidence to the conclusion directly. When an argument says something was *impossible*, look for the answer that rules out one more way it could have happened.\n\n**(D) Not Necessary.**\nA common myth would *help* Mikkeli by explaining the similarities innocently. But his defense doesn't depend on it. His argument is about access: he couldn't have known the book. Negate (D), so there's no common myth, and his access argument is exactly as strong as before.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.**\nThis is the tempting one because it sounds like another language door. But Old Icelandic is extinct and only related to an *earlier* form of Norwegian. Negate it, so Mikkeli knows Old Icelandic, and he still can't read modern Norwegian. Halden's book was published 20 years before his, not 800. Knowing an ancient cousin of the language doesn't let him read the book.\n\n---\n\n## 11. PT114-S2-Q21 · Necessary Assumption · Difficulty 4 · Answer C\n\n> So-called \"engineered foods,\" usually in powder or liquid form, consist of protein that is distilled from natural sources and supplemented with vitamins and minerals. Although the amino acids contained in such products stimulate the production of growth hormones, these hormones produce growth in connective tissue rather than in muscle mass; this does not improve muscle strength. Hence, athletes, who need to improve their muscular strength, should not consume engineered foods.\n>\n> The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?\n>\n> (A) An increase in muscle mass produces an increase in strength. · (B) People who are not athletes require neither stronger connective tissue nor muscle strength. · (C) If an engineered food does not improve muscle strength, there is no other substantial advantage to athletes from consuming it. · (D) Consuming engineered foods that provide nutrients that can be obtained more easily elsewhere is unhealthy. · (E) Growth of muscle mass enhances muscle strength only when accompanied by growth of connective tissue.\n\nA 26% · B 0% · C 71% · D 1% · E 2%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (hence)**\nAthletes should not consume engineered foods.\n\n**Evidence**\n- Engineered foods are protein plus vitamins and minerals.\n- Their amino acids stimulate growth hormones, but those hormones grow connective tissue, not muscle mass.\n- That doesn't improve muscle strength.\n- Athletes need to improve their muscle strength.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThe evidence shows that engineered foods won't do one thing: build muscle strength. The conclusion is that athletes shouldn't eat them at all.\n\nThat's a jump. \"This doesn't help with X\" is not the same as \"you shouldn't use this.\"\n\n*Given that ...* engineered foods don't improve muscle strength,\n  *How could we argue that ...* athletes should still consume them?\n  - They're protein with vitamins and minerals. Maybe they help with recovery, energy, or general nutrition.\n  - Stronger connective tissue sounds like it might prevent injuries. Plenty of athletes would want that.\n  - Maybe they're just a convenient way to get calories during training.\n\nAny real benefit could make them worth eating, even if they don't build strength. When an argument recommends against a plan because of one missing benefit, it has to assume there's no other benefit that tips the scale.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for a defender: an answer that says engineered foods offer athletes no other significant benefit. Negate it and we should get \"they do have another real benefit,\" which kills the \"should not consume\" conclusion.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not Necessary.**\nThis is the big trap, and it feels necessary because it seems to be the logic behind the premise. But look at what the author actually *says*: the hormones grow connective tissue rather than muscle, and \"this does not improve muscle strength.\" The author asserts that engineered foods don't improve strength. The argument doesn't need a separate rule about muscle mass to get there.\n\nRun the negation test: an increase in muscle mass does *not* produce an increase in strength. Does that make engineered foods any better for athletes? No. They still don't grow muscle, and they still don't improve strength. The argument is untouched.\n\nThe gap on this question is between the evidence and the conclusion (no strength benefit → don't eat them), not inside the evidence.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nThe argument is only about athletes. What non-athletes need tells us nothing about whether athletes should consume these foods. Negate it (some non-athletes need stronger connective tissue) and the argument about athletes is unaffected.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\nNegate it: even if an engineered food doesn't improve strength, athletes *do* get some other substantial advantage from it. Now \"athletes should not consume engineered foods\" falls apart. Maybe they should eat them for that other advantage.\n\nThis is the defender we predicted. Whenever the conclusion is a recommendation (should / should not), check whether the author has weighed *all* the effects, or just one.\n\n**(D) Not Necessary.**\nThe argument never says engineered foods are unhealthy, or that their nutrients are available more easily elsewhere. Its only reason is that they don't build strength. Negate (D) so these foods are perfectly healthy, and the author's reason still stands.\n\n**(E) Not Necessary.**\nThis is a claim about how muscle mass and connective tissue work together. The argument never relies on it. Negate it (muscle growth can boost strength even without connective tissue growth) and nothing changes, because engineered foods don't produce muscle growth in the first place.\n\n---\n\n## 12. PT114-S4-Q12 · Sufficient Assumption · Difficulty 2 · Answer E\n\n> Morris: Computers, despite some people's expectations, will have an inappreciable impact on education. To be sure, computers are useful for drills promoting memorization, though only a small part of education can be accomplished through drills. But machines cannot help students with any of the higher intellectual functions we call understanding; for that, human teachers are indispensable.\n>\n> The conclusion of Morris's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?\n>\n> (A) Whatever memorization is necessary can be accomplished as easily without computers as with them. · (B) Requiring memorization in appreciable amounts tends to thwart development of higher intellectual functions in students. · (C) Successful memorization of relevant facts is a necessary precondition for the development of higher intellectual functions in students. · (D) Many students become familiar with computers before encountering them at school. · (E) Having an appreciable impact on education involves affecting the higher intellectual functions of students.\n\nA 5% · B 5% · C 7% · D 0% · E 83%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nComputers will have an inappreciable impact on education.\n\n**Evidence**\n- Computers help with memorization drills, but drills are only a small part of education.\n- Computers can't help with the higher intellectual functions (understanding). Only human teachers can.\n\n**Evaluate**\nMorris's conclusion uses a concept the evidence never mentions: an \"appreciable impact on education.\" The evidence talks about drills and higher intellectual functions. Nothing tells us what it takes to have an appreciable impact.\n\nSo we need a bridge. Think of it as subtraction. Take what's in the conclusion but not the evidence (appreciable impact), and connect it to what's in the evidence that points the right way (computers can't help with higher functions).\n\n  *Can't help with higher functions → inappreciable impact*\n\nOr, flipped around into its contrapositive:\n\n  *Appreciable impact → helps with higher functions*\n\nEither version finishes the argument. If an appreciable impact requires touching the higher functions, and computers can't touch them, computers can't have an appreciable impact.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer that says an appreciable impact on education requires affecting students' higher intellectual functions (or its contrapositive: without affecting them, there's no appreciable impact).\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not Sufficient.**\nThis one closes a door: computers don't even add anything to memorization. But it doesn't close all of them. Computers could still have an appreciable impact on education some other way we haven't considered: organizing information, motivating students, connecting them to teachers. Morris needs a rule that says the *only* route to appreciable impact is through the higher functions. (A) doesn't give us that.\n\n**(B) Goes the Wrong Way.**\nIf lots of memorization actually *hurts* the development of higher functions, and computers push memorization drills, then computers might have a big (bad) impact on education. That's an appreciable impact, which works against Morris.\n\n**(C) Goes the Wrong Way.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer. If memorization is a necessary step toward higher functions, then computers, which help with memorization, might be helping indirectly with understanding after all. That opens a door to computers having an appreciable impact. Morris wants that door shut.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.**\nWhen students first meet computers says nothing about whether computers will have an appreciable impact on their education.\n\n**(E) Correct.**\nThis is the contrapositive version of our bridge:\n  *Appreciable impact on education → affects higher intellectual functions*\n\nComputers can't help with the higher functions, so they fail the requirement, so they can't have an appreciable impact. The conclusion is now proven.\n\nOn Sufficient Assumption, when the conclusion has a concept the evidence never mentions (\"appreciable impact\"), the right answer almost always defines that new concept in terms of something the evidence did cover.\n\n---\n\n## 13. PT105-S1-Q3 · Strengthen · Difficulty 1 · Answer C\n\n> Space programs have recently suffered several setbacks with respect to their large projects, and much money has been lost. Consequently, these grand projects should be abandoned in favor of several small ones.\n>\n> Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the reasoning above?\n>\n> (A) The cost of starting a space project increases every year. · (B) It is just as easy to revise, and even scrap, small projects as it is large ones. · (C) Large projects are intrinsically more likely to fail and so are more financially risky than small projects. · (D) Project managers prefer to work on small projects rather than large ones. · (E) Large space projects can explore a few places thoroughly, while small projects can investigate more regions, though less thoroughly.\n\nA 1% · B 2% · C 96% · D 1% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (consequently)**\nSpace programs should abandon their large projects in favor of several small ones.\n\n**Evidence**\nLarge space projects have had several recent setbacks, and much money has been lost.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThe author is recommending a switch: large projects out, small projects in. But the only evidence is that large projects have been going badly.\n\n*Given that ...* large projects have lost a lot of money,\n  *How could we argue that ...* we still shouldn't switch to small ones?\n  - Maybe small projects would lose even more money, or fail just as often.\n  - Maybe the recent setbacks were bad luck, not something about being large.\n\nThe author is assuming small projects would do better. To strengthen, we want a reason to believe that: some difference between large and small projects that makes large ones the problem.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer that says large projects, because they're large, are more likely to fail or waste money than small ones.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Distinction.**\nRising start-up costs apply to *every* space project, large or small. That doesn't give us a reason to prefer one over the other. (If anything, starting *several* small projects means paying that rising start-up cost several times.)\n\n**(B) Weakens.**\nIf small projects are just as easy to scrap as large ones, that removes one possible advantage of going small. This pulls the two options closer together, which doesn't help an argument that says one is better.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\nThis is the difference we were looking for. Large projects are *intrinsically* more likely to fail, so they're riskier with money. Now the recent setbacks aren't bad luck. They're what you'd expect from large projects, and small ones would be safer.\n\nWhenever an argument recommends switching from one option to another, the best strengtheners give a reason the new option is actually better on the thing the evidence complained about. Here, that's failure and lost money.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.**\nWhat project managers like to work on doesn't tell us which projects succeed or lose money. The argument is about setbacks and money, not job satisfaction.\n\n**(E) Unclear Impact.**\nThis is a trade-off: large projects go deep, small ones go wide. It doesn't say either approach avoids setbacks or saves money, and it doesn't say which is better. We can't tell whether this makes the switch look good or bad.\n\n---\n\n## 14. PT120-S4-Q9 · Principle-Strengthen · Difficulty 2 · Answer C\n\n> Writer: I collaborated with another writer on my last book, instead of writing alone as I usually do. Because the book sold so well as a result of this joint effort, I should collaborate with a writer on my next book so that book will sell well too.\n>\n> Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?\n>\n> (A) If a person's book sells well because of a collaboration, that person's next book will sell well, if he or she collaborates with the same writer. · (B) A book sells well only if its author collaborated on the book with another writer. · (C) If a person's book sells well because of a collaboration, future collaborations on the part of that person will produce other books that sell well. · (D) Writers who do not collaborate on books have a smaller chance of writing a book that will sell well. · (E) Writers who collaborate on books, if they are good writers, usually produce books that sell well.\n\nA 5% · B 7% · C 84% · D 2% · E 2%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nI should collaborate with a writer on my next book, so that it will sell well too.\n\n**Evidence**\nMy last book was a collaboration, and it sold well *because* of that collaboration.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThis is \"it worked last time, so it'll work next time.\" Plenty could go wrong with that:\n- Maybe it only worked because of *that particular* co-writer.\n- Maybe the topic was hot that year.\n- Maybe collaborations help once, but readers get tired of them.\n\nA principle that justifies this needs to promise that if collaboration made one book sell well, collaborating again will make the next one sell well. It should also cover *any* collaboration, since the writer's conclusion is \"collaborate with a writer,\" not \"collaborate with the same writer.\"\n\n**Goal**\nBuild it as \"if evidence, then conclusion\":\n  *If your book sold well because of a collaboration → your future collaborations will produce books that sell well*\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Trigger Match.**\nClose, but (A) only promises success if the writer works with *the same* co-writer. The writer's conclusion is to collaborate with \"a writer,\" any writer. (A) can't justify that, because it says nothing about what happens with a new partner. A principle can only prove what's on its right-hand side, and here the right-hand side is narrower than the conclusion.\n\n**(B) Doesn't Justify the Conclusion.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer. It says collaboration is *necessary* for a book to sell well. So yes, if the writer wants the next book to sell well, he'd better collaborate.\n\nBut look at the whole conclusion: collaborate \"so that book *will* sell well.\" (B) never promises that collaborating leads to good sales. It only says you can't sell well without it. Collaboration could be necessary and still not enough.\n\n(B) also ignores the writer's evidence completely. His reasoning is \"collaboration caused my last book to sell well.\" (B) would make that evidence pointless.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\nThis is our prediction almost word for word:\n- \"If a person's book sells well because of a collaboration\": the writer's last book.\n- \"future collaborations on the part of that person will produce other books that sell well\": collaborate on the next book, and it will sell well.\n\nThe trigger matches the evidence exactly, and the outcome matches the conclusion exactly.\n\n**(D) Too Weak.**\nA \"smaller chance\" of selling well without collaboration doesn't mean collaboration will make the next book sell well. It only compares odds. The writer's conclusion is confident: the next book *will* sell well.\n\n**(E) Bad Trigger Match.**\n(E) only kicks in for \"good writers,\" and we don't know whether our writer is one. It also only promises books \"usually\" sell well, which is weaker than the writer's conclusion. Two strikes.\n\n---\n\n## 15. PT105-S4-Q12 · Principle-Conform · Difficulty 2 · Answer A\n\n> Nearly everyone has complained of a mistaken utility bill that cannot easily be corrected or of computer files that cannot readily be retrieved. Yet few people today would tolerate waiting in long lines while clerks search for information that can now be found in seconds, and almost no one who has used a word processor would return to a typewriter.\n>\n> The information above conforms most closely to which one of the following principles?\n>\n> (A) The fact that people complain about some consequences of technology cannot be taken as a reliable indication that they would choose to live without it. · (B) If people do not complain about some technology, then it is probably not a significant factor in their daily lives. · (C) The degree to which technologies elicit complaints from people is always an accurate measure of the extent to which people have become dependent on them. · (D) The complaints people make about technological innovations are more reliable evidence of the importance of those innovations than the choices people actually make. · (E) The less willing people are to do without technology the more likely they are to complain about the effects of technology.\n\nA 84% · B 1% · C 4% · D 5% · E 5%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements**\n- Nearly everyone has complained about some technology problem (a billing error, lost computer files).\n- *Yet* hardly anyone would go back to waiting in long lines for clerks, and almost no one would give up a word processor for a typewriter.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThis isn't an argument. There's no conclusion. It's two observations joined by \"yet,\" and the pivot tells us they pull against each other.\n\nWhat's the tension? People complain about technology all the time. But when it comes down to it, they wouldn't give it up.\n\nIf we had to put that in a slogan: *People gripe about technology, but they wouldn't live without it.*\n\n**Goal**\nLook for a principle that says complaints about technology don't mean people would actually choose to go without it. The right answer will match both halves: complaints on one side, the choice to keep the technology on the other.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\nThis is our slogan in formal clothes:\n- \"people complain about some consequences of technology\": billing errors and lost files.\n- \"cannot be taken as a reliable indication that they would choose to live without it\": no one's going back to typewriters.\n\nOn Conform questions without a conclusion, boil the stimulus down to one sentence first. Then the right principle is usually easy to spot.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nThe stimulus is about technology people *do* complain about. It says nothing about technology people don't complain about, so it can't illustrate a rule about that group.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.**\n\"Always an accurate measure\" is extreme. And the stimulus actually points the other way: complaints *don't* tell you how people really feel about technology. Everyone complains, but their choices show they depend on it anyway.\n\n**(D) Reversed.**\nThe stimulus suggests the opposite: people's choices (keeping the word processor) tell you more than their complaints. (D) says complaints are the better evidence.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.**\nThis is a sliding scale: the more you depend on technology, the more you complain. The stimulus never compares degrees. It just says nearly everyone complains and nearly everyone would keep the technology. Nothing about more of one producing more of the other.\n\n---\n\n## 16. PT116-S2-Q19 · Agree · Difficulty 3 · Answer D\n\n> Marc: The fact that the people of our country look back on the past with a great deal of nostalgia demonstrates that they regret the recent revolution.\n>\n> Robert: They are not nostalgic for the recent past, but for the distant past, which the prerevolutionary regime despised; this indicates that although they are troubled, they do not regret the revolution.\n>\n> Their dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Marc and Robert agree that the people of their country\n>\n> (A) tend to underrate past problems when the country faces troubling times · (B) are looking to the past for solutions to the country's current problems · (C) are likely to repeat former mistakes if they look to the country's past for solutions to current problems · (D) are concerned about the country's current situation and this is evidenced by their nostalgia · (E) tend to be most nostalgic for the things that are the farthest in their past\n\nA 5% · B 8% · C 1% · D 77% · E 9%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Marc's Claims**\n1. The people look back on the past with a lot of nostalgia.\n2. That nostalgia shows they regret the recent revolution.\n\n**Does Robert Agree?**\n1. The people are nostalgic? **Yes.** He says they're nostalgic for the *distant* past, not the recent one. He's correcting *what* they're nostalgic for, not *whether* they're nostalgic.\n2. The nostalgia shows they regret the revolution? **No.** That's his whole point. He thinks the nostalgia shows they're troubled, but not that they regret the revolution.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThis is an Agree question, so we're hunting for common ground. Both speakers read the nostalgia as a sign of something going on with the people now:\n- Marc: it shows they regret the revolution. You don't regret something unless you're unhappy with where it's left you.\n- Robert: it shows \"they are troubled.\"\n\nSo they share a starting point: the people are nostalgic, and that nostalgia tells us something is bothering them about the present. They only split on what exactly that something is.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer that says the people are unhappy or concerned about their present situation, and that their nostalgia is the sign of it. Stay away from anything specific to only one speaker: the revolution (Marc) or the distant past (Robert).\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported Agree Position.**\nNeither speaker says the people underrate past problems. Robert does note they're nostalgic for a past the old regime despised, but that's not the same as saying they're forgetting the problems of that time. Neither speaker takes a position on this.\n\n**(B) Unsupported Agree Position.**\nNeither speaker mentions solutions. Nostalgia is about longing for the past, not about using the past to fix the present. We can't put either speaker behind this.\n\n**(C) Unsupported Agree Position.**\nSame problem as (B), and worse: neither speaker says anything about repeating mistakes.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nCheck both speakers:\n- **Robert:** explicitly says the nostalgia \"indicates that ... they are troubled.\" Concerned about their current situation, shown by the nostalgia. Yes.\n- **Marc:** says the nostalgia demonstrates they regret the recent revolution. Regretting the revolution means being unhappy with what it's brought, which is the country's current situation. Yes.\n\nThey disagree about *why* the people are troubled, but they agree *that* they are, and that the nostalgia shows it.\n\n**(E) Unsupported Agree Position.**\nThis is the most tempting wrong answer, because Robert does say the people are nostalgic for the distant past. But Marc never says which part of the past. And \"most nostalgic for the things that are the farthest\" is a ranking neither of them makes. Robert only says distant rather than recent, not that the farther back, the stronger the nostalgia.\n\n---\n\n## 17. PT128-S3-Q16 · Main Conclusion · Difficulty 2 · Answer D\n\n*Not loaded yet.*\n\n> The primary task of a university is to educate. But to teach well, professors must be informed about new developments in their disciplines, and that requires research. Yet many universities cannot afford to support faculty research adequately. So a lack of funds for research adversely affects the degree to which a university can fulfill its central mission.\n>\n> Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion of the argument?\n>\n> (A) In order to be able to teach well, university professors must conduct research. · (B) Lack of financial support for faculty research is the root of ineffective teaching at universities. · (C) Effective teaching is the primary mission of a university. · (D) Lack of funds for research reduces the quality of education a university provides. · (E) New means of funding faculty research at universities are needed.\n\nA 4% · B 7% · C 3% · D 85% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (so)**\nA lack of research funding hurts a university's ability to fulfill its central mission. Rephrase: *a lack of research funding hurts a university's ability to educate.*\n\n**Evidence**\n- A university's primary task is to educate.\n- To teach well, professors have to keep up with new developments, which requires research.\n- Many universities can't afford to support research properly.\n\n**Evaluate**\nMost of the time on Main Conclusion questions, the conclusion is the first sentence or comes right after a pivot. It's the final sentence only about 10% of the time. This is one of those times, and it's safe to say so here because:\n- \"So\" introduces it.\n- Nothing comes after it to support it.\n- Every earlier sentence feeds into it. The first sentence tells us what the \"central mission\" is, the second links teaching to research, and the third says research is underfunded.\n\nAlso notice the referential language. \"Its central mission\" only makes sense if we go back to the first sentence: the mission is to educate.\n\n**Goal**\nSwap the reference for the specific word, then look for the closest match: *lack of research funding hurts how well a university can educate.*\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Premise.**\nThis restates the second sentence: teaching well requires keeping up, which requires research. It's support for the conclusion, not the conclusion. Ask \"why should we believe this?\" and the argument gives no answer; it just asserts it.\n\n**(B) Too Strong.**\n\"The root of ineffective teaching\" says lack of funding is *the* cause of bad teaching. The author only says lack of funding *adversely affects* education, which leaves room for many other causes. (B) turns \"one thing that hurts\" into \"the source of the problem.\"\n\n**(C) Premise.**\nThis is the first sentence, reworded. It's there to tell us what \"central mission\" means. (It also slightly shifts \"educate\" to \"effective teaching.\") It's support, not the conclusion.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nLine it up:\n- \"Lack of funds for research\": a lack of funds for research.\n- \"reduces the quality of education a university provides\": adversely affects how well a university fulfills its central mission (educating).\n\nThe only work required is swapping \"central mission\" for \"education,\" which is exactly what the Goal step set up.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.**\nThe author never proposes a fix. She only says underfunding hurts education. Calling for new funding sources goes one step further than the argument ever does.\n\n---\n\n## 18. PT105-S1-Q11 · Role · Difficulty 3 · Answer E\n\n> Although the concept of free will is essential to that of moral responsibility, its role in determining responsibility is not the same in all situations. We hold criminals morally responsible for the damage they cause, assuming that they freely chose their activities. But we do not hold someone who has a heart attack while driving morally responsible for the damage caused, if any, even when we have good reason to believe that the heart attack could have been prevented by eating different foods and that one's choice of diet is made freely.\n>\n> The claim that a choice of diet can affect whether or not one has a heart attack plays which one of the following roles in the argument?\n>\n> (A) It is a subsidiary conclusion of the argument. · (B) It is used to show that we should hold someone morally responsible for damages caused by having a heart attack while driving. · (C) It is cited as evidence that our concept of moral responsibility should be the same in all situations. · (D) It is used to disprove the claim that we should not hold criminals morally responsible for damages. · (E) It is used in support of the conclusion of the argument.\n\nA 6% · B 3% · C 11% · D 3% · E 77%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nFree will is essential to moral responsibility, but it doesn't play the same role in every situation.\n\n**Evidence**\n- Criminals: we hold them responsible, because they freely chose what they did.\n- Heart attack drivers: we *don't* hold them responsible, even when a freely chosen diet could have prevented the heart attack.\n\n**Evaluate**\nFirst sentence, and after \"although\": that's where the conclusion usually lives, and it does here. The rest of the paragraph is two examples that show free will working differently in two cases.\n\nWhere does the diet claim fit? It's part of the second example. It's what makes the heart attack case interesting. The driver made a free choice (their diet) that led to the damage, just like a criminal. And yet we don't blame them.\n\nWithout the diet claim, the heart attack example proves nothing. \"We don't blame people for random heart attacks\" doesn't show free will working differently, because there'd be no free choice involved at all. The diet claim is what sneaks free will into the heart attack case, so the contrast with criminals actually works.\n\nIs anything offered to *support* the diet claim? No. The author just says we have good reason to believe it. It isn't concluded from anything.\n\n**Goal**\nThe diet claim is a premise. It supports the main conclusion by setting up a case where free choice was involved but we still don't assign responsibility.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not a Conclusion.**\nA subsidiary conclusion has to be supported by something and then support something else. Ask \"why should we believe the diet can affect heart attacks?\" The argument doesn't say. It's just given. So it's a premise, not a conclusion.\n\n**(B) Opposite.**\nThe argument says we do *not* hold heart attack drivers responsible. The diet claim is part of showing that we don't blame them *even though* free choice was involved. (B) has it pointing the opposite way.\n\n**(C) Opposite.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer, and it's the conclusion flipped around. The author argues free will's role is *not* the same in all situations. The diet claim helps show that difference. (C) says it shows everything should be the same, which is the opposite of the point.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.**\nThe argument never disputes that criminals should be held responsible. It agrees they should. And the diet claim is about heart attacks, not criminals.\n\n**(E) Correct.**\nThe diet claim is support. It's what puts a free choice into the heart attack example, so that the example can show free will doesn't always lead to responsibility. That supports the main conclusion that free will's role isn't the same in all situations.\n\nOn Role questions, \"used in support of the conclusion\" can feel too plain to be right. But when the claim is a premise with nothing supporting it, the plain answer is often exactly the right one.\n\n---\n\n## 19. PT115-S2-Q8 · Parallel · Difficulty 2 · Answer B\n\n> The kind of thoughts that keep a person from falling asleep can arise in either half of the brain. Therefore, a person being prevented from sleeping solely by such thoughts would be able to fall asleep by closing the eyes and counting sheep, because this activity fully occupies the left half of the brain with counting and the right half of the brain with imagining sheep, thereby excluding the sleep-preventing thoughts.\n>\n> Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning in the argument above?\n>\n> (A) Stucco is a poor insulator but brick and wood are good insulators, so a person who wants to build a house in an area with a cold climate should use brick or wood instead of stucco. · (B) Cats can damage furniture with either their claws or their teeth, so such damage can be prevented by providing cats with other objects that they will claw and bite, such as toy mice. · (C) This map indicates two roads of equal length each leading to Centreville, so a person who wants to take the shortest route to Centreville could choose either one. · (D) These chemicals are harmless by themselves but explosive when mixed together, so in order to be kept in the same laboratory without risk, they should be stored separately. · (E) This island has two harbors but one of them is too shallow to permit large ships, so this ship will have to dock in the other harbor in order to unload its cargo.\n\nA 4% · B 87% · C 1% · D 6% · E 2%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (therefore)**\nCounting sheep would let a person fall asleep, if sleep-preventing thoughts are the only thing keeping them awake.\n\n**Evidence**\n- Sleep-preventing thoughts can come from either half of the brain.\n- Counting sheep fully occupies both halves (left counts, right imagines sheep), so there's no room left for those thoughts.\n\n**Evaluate**\nStrip out the brains and sheep and look at the story:\n1. A problem can come from two sources.\n2. One activity keeps *both* sources busy.\n3. So that activity prevents the problem.\n\nThat's the recipe. A problem with two sources, blocked by an activity that occupies both at once. No need to diagram formally here. The shape is simple enough to match in plain language.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer where something bad can come from either of two sources, and the fix is to keep both of those sources busy with something harmless.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Structure Match.**\nThis is a choice between materials: one's bad, two are good, so pick a good one. There's no single activity occupying two sources of a problem. It's just picking the better option.\n\n**(B) Correct.**\nMap it:\n- Problem: furniture damage. (Sleeplessness.)\n- Two sources: claws or teeth. (Left or right half of the brain.)\n- One activity that occupies both: toy mice to claw *and* bite. (Counting sheep, which uses both halves.)\n- So the problem is prevented.\n\nEvery piece lines up, including the idea that the fix works by giving each source something else to do.\n\n**(C) Bad Structure Match.**\nTwo equal routes, so either works. There's no problem being blocked and nothing being kept busy. The \"two\" here is two options, not two sources of trouble.\n\n**(D) Bad Structure Match.**\nThis is the most tempting wrong answer, because it also has two things and a way to prevent harm. But the structure is different. In (D), the problem only happens when the two chemicals come *together*, and the fix is to keep them *apart*. In the original, each source can cause the problem on its own, and the fix is to keep *both* occupied. Separating vs. occupying: different recipe.\n\n**(E) Bad Structure Match.**\nTwo harbors, one ruled out, so use the other. That's process of elimination, not blocking a problem at two sources.\n\n---\n\n## 20. PT104-S4-Q13 · Parallel Flaw · Difficulty 4 · Answer D\n\n> Historian: The ancient Greeks failed to recognize that, morally, democracy is no improvement over monarchy. It is wrong for an individual to have the power to choose the course of action for a government, so it is no less wrong to grant this power to society, which is just a collection of individuals.\n>\n> The pattern of flawed reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?\n>\n> (A) There is no point in trying to find someone else to solve that problem. If Robin cannot solve it, then none of Robin's friends would be able to solve it. · (B) We should not pick Hank for the relay team. He has not won a race all season, so there is no reason to expect him to help the relay team win. · (C) Laws that contain exemptions for some individuals based on no relevant consideration are fundamentally immoral. If it is wrong for a given person to commit an act, then it is wrong for anyone else in similar circumstances to commit the act. · (D) There is no point in asking the club to purchase tents and make them available for use by club members. No member of the club can afford one of those tents, so the club is unable to afford any either. · (E) Agreeing with all of the other members of society does not guarantee that one is correct about an issue. With many topics it is possible for society to be mistaken and hence every individual in society to be likewise mistaken.\n\nA 5% · B 2% · C 17% · D 66% · E 10%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nMorally, democracy is no improvement over monarchy. (The Greeks were wrong to think otherwise.)\n\n**Intermediate Conclusion (so)**\nIt's no less wrong to give the power to run the government to society.\n\n**Evidence**\n- It's wrong for one individual to have the power to choose the government's course.\n- Society is just a collection of individuals.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThe historian takes something true of each *individual* and assumes it's true of the *group* they make up. That's the part-to-whole flaw.\n\nWhy doesn't it work? Groups can have properties their members don't. One person running the country might be wrong because it's one unchecked person. A whole society deciding together has checks, debate and majority votes. The very thing that made it wrong for the individual could be missing for the group.\n\nEveryday version: one brick can't hold up a roof. Many bricks together can. You can't reason from \"each piece can't\" to \"the whole can't.\"\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer that goes from a property of each member to the same property for the group, in that direction: part to whole. Watch out for answers that go whole to part, or individual to other individuals. Those have a different shape even if they feel similar.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Flaw Match.**\nRobin can't solve it, so Robin's friends can't either. That's going from one individual to *other* individuals, not from members to the group they form. It's a flawed argument, but it's a different flaw (assuming Robin's friends are no better than Robin).\n\n**(B) Bad Flaw Match.**\nHank hasn't won a race, so he won't help the relay team win. It's reasoning about one person's contribution to a team. It doesn't say \"each member can't, so the team can't.\" (And there's a decent argument that a runner who never wins won't help much, so it's not even clearly flawed the same way.)\n\n**(C) Bad Flaw Match.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer, because it talks about individuals and wrongness, just like the historian. But look at the direction. It goes from what's wrong for *one person* to what's wrong for *other people in similar circumstances*. That's individual to individual, not individual to group. It's also a pretty reasonable principle, not a flaw at all.\n\nParallel Flaw questions love a wrong answer that copies the *topic*. Match the flaw, not the vocabulary.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\n- No individual member can afford a tent. (No individual should have the power.)\n- So the club, a collection of members, can't afford one either. (So society, a collection of individuals, shouldn't have it either.)\n\nSame flaw, same direction: part to whole. And it fails for the same reason. Members can pool their money, just like a society can pool its judgment. What's true of each piece isn't necessarily true of the whole.\n\n**(E) Bad Flaw Match.**\nThis goes the other direction: the whole society might be mistaken, so every individual is mistaken. Whole to part. That's a flaw too (called division), but it's the mirror image of the historian's. It also concludes that being mistaken is *possible*, which is much weaker than the historian's firm conclusion.\n"}
