Any O'Brien student who heard it from the beginning *would* have found it fascinating. So if an O'Brien student had heard it from the beginning, that student would be exactly the kind of person (D) says doesn't exist. The only way (D) and the rule can both be true is if no O'Brien student heard it from the beginning.\n\nThat makes the conclusion false while both premises still stand: the fascinated students must have come in late. That's the world we predicted.\n\n**(E) Bad Objection.**\nDisruptions affect who heard the *entire* lecture. The argument is about who heard the *beginning*. Someone who arrived on time and then got distracted by latecomers still heard the start. (E) doesn't stop any O'Brien student from hearing the beginning, so the conclusion survives.\n\n---\n\n## 4. PT104-S4-Q23 · Most Supported · Difficulty 2 · Answer E\n\n*Modelled on PT151-S3-Q14 (Most Supported, Important Pivot) and PT155-S1-Q15.*\n\n> Much of today's literature is inferior: most of our authors are intellectually and emotionally inexperienced, and their works lack both the intricacy and the focus on the significant that characterize good literature. However, Hypatia's latest novel is promising; it shows a maturity, complexity, and grace that far exceeds that of her earlier works.\n>\n> Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?\n>\n> (A) Much of today's literature focuses less on the significant than Hypatia's latest novel focuses on the significant. · (B) Much of today's literature at least lacks the property of grace. · (C) Hypatia's latest novel is good literature when judged by today's standards. · (D) Hypatia's latest novel is clearly better than the majority of today's literature. · (E) Hypatia's latest novel has at least one property of good literature to a greater degree than her earlier works.\n\nA 6% · B 2% · C 4% · D 4% · E 84%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements**\n  - Much of today's literature is inferior.\n  - Most of today's authors are intellectually and emotionally inexperienced.\n  - Their works lack intricacy and a focus on the significant, which are what characterize good literature.\n  - *pivot (however)*\n  - Hypatia's latest novel is promising: it shows maturity, complexity and grace far beyond her *earlier works*.\n\n**Evaluate**\nWhen we read Inference paragraphs, we hunt for claims that can be combined, usually through an Overlapping Idea. We also watch for Conditional, Causal and Mathematical wording, and for a paragraph that Ends with a Pivot.\n\nThis one ends with a pivot, so our job is usually to reconcile the last idea with what came before it.\n\nWhere's the overlap? Good literature has *intricacy*. Hypatia's new novel has more *complexity*. Intricacy and complexity are close enough to be the same property. So her new novel has more of one of the things good literature has.\n\nNow notice what Hypatia's novel is compared to. Not today's literature. Her own earlier books. That limits what we can say. And \"promising\" is the author holding back on purpose. Promising isn't good.\n\n**Goal**\nWe want a safely worded answer that combines the two halves: Hypatia's latest novel has more of a good-literature trait (complexity/intricacy) than her earlier work. Be suspicious of anything that ranks her against other authors or calls her novel good literature.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported Comparison.**\nWe have no idea whether Hypatia's new novel focuses on the significant at all. The passage credits it with maturity, complexity and grace. \"Focus on the significant\" isn't on that list, so we can't say she beats anyone on that score.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.**\nToday's works are said to lack intricacy and a focus on the significant. Grace only shows up in the description of Hypatia's novel. Nothing tells us the rest of today's literature lacks it.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.**\n\"Promising\" is not \"good.\" All we know is that the new book beats Hypatia's earlier books. If her earlier books were terrible, \"much better than terrible\" can still fall short of good literature.\n\n**(D) Unsupported Comparison.**\nTwo problems. The only comparison in the passage is to her *earlier* works, not to today's literature. And \"much\" of today's literature is inferior, which isn't the same as \"the majority.\" A lot of trap answers take an absolute idea and turn it into a comparison the passage never made.\n\n**(E) Correct.**\nThis is the most safely worded answer available. It stays inside the one comparison we actually have (new novel vs. her earlier works) and only claims *at least one* property. Complexity is that property: it matches the intricacy that characterizes good literature, and her new novel has more of it.\n\nOn Most Supported, \"at least one,\" \"some\" and \"can\" are good signs. The right answer usually claims just enough to be backed by the passage.\n\n---\n\n## 5. PT109-S3-Q3 · Paradox EXCEPT · Difficulty 1 · Answer B\n\n*Modelled on PT112-S4-Q5 (Paradox EXCEPT: \"Our job here ...\" on every note) and PT106-S2-Q26.*\n\n> The most common bird in Stillwater Marsh is a species of marsh hen, yet this species is rarely seen, even by experienced bird-watchers who seek it. In fact, this bird is seen far less frequently than any other bird inhabiting the marsh, including those that are much smaller and much less abundant.\n>\n> Each of the following, if true, helps to reconcile the statements above except:\n>\n> (A) The coloration of the marsh hen blends in particularly well with the marsh grass where the marsh hen nests. · (B) The marsh hen's call is harsh and repetitive, whereas the calls of many other marsh birds are pleasant and melodious. · (C) Unlike many small marsh birds, which dash along the banks of the marsh, the marsh hen remains completely still for long periods of time. · (D) Many marsh birds are most active during daylight hours, but the marsh hen is usually most active at night. · (E) Although many small marsh birds fly in groups to several feeding areas each day, the marsh hen tends to be solitary and flies only when it is in danger.\n\nA 3% · B 92% · C 2% · D 2% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that ...**\nThe marsh hen is the most common bird in Stillwater Marsh.\n\n**How can it be that ...**\nIt's seen less often than any other bird there, including smaller and rarer ones, even by experienced bird-watchers looking for it?\n\n**Evaluate**\nWe'd expect the most common bird to be the one people see most. So something about the marsh hen must make it hard to *see*, no matter how many there are.\n\nWhat makes a bird hard to spot? It blends in. It doesn't move. It's out when people aren't. It stays hidden and rarely flies.\n\nOn EXCEPT questions, the four answers we eliminate usually come at the paradox from the same angle. Here that angle is \"the marsh hen is hard to see.\"\n\n**Goal**\nEliminate four answers that give the marsh hen a reason to be hard to see. The correct answer will be neutral (nothing to do with being seen) or it will make the hen *easier* to notice.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Helps Explain.**\nOur job here: given that the marsh hen is the most common bird, why is it rarely seen?\n\nThis answer says, \"It's rarely seen because it's camouflaged in the grass where it nests.\" You can walk past a hundred of them and never see one.\n\n**(B) Correct.**\nOur job here: given that the marsh hen is the most common bird, why is it rarely seen?\n\nThis answer says, \"It's rarely seen because its call is harsh.\" That doesn't connect. A call is something you *hear*. And a harsh, repetitive call would, if anything, help a bird-watcher locate the hen, not hide it. This is the exception.\n\nWhen an EXCEPT answer is about a different sense or a different kind of evidence than the paradox (hearing vs. seeing), it's usually the one that doesn't help.\n\n**(C) Helps Explain.**\nThis answer says, \"It's rarely seen because it sits frozen while the small birds dash around.\" Movement catches the eye. Still birds are much harder to spot.\n\n**(D) Helps Explain.**\nThis answer says, \"It's rarely seen because it's active at night, while bird-watchers are out during the day.\"\n\n**(E) Helps Explain.**\nThis answer says, \"It's rarely seen because it stays alone and only flies when it's in danger, while the small birds fly around in groups all day.\" Flocks in the air are easy to spot. A bird that stays hidden in the grass isn't.\n\n---\n\n## 6. PT108-S3-Q6 · Paradox EXCEPT · Difficulty 4 · Answer C\n\n*Breakdown only. This question already has LSAT Lab's five Choice Notes, which stay as they are. Modelled on PT112-S4-Q5 (the \"3 of 4 from one angle\" setup) and PT126-S4-Q5.*\n\n> Shortly after the power plant opened and began discharging its wastewater into the river, there was a decrease in the overall number of bass caught by anglers downstream from the plant.\n>\n> Each of the following, if true, could explain the decrease described above EXCEPT:\n>\n> (A) The discharged wastewater made the river more attractive to fish that are the natural predators of bass. · (B) The discharged water was warmer than the normal river temperature, leading the bass to seek cooler water elsewhere. · (C) Because of the new plant, access to the part of the river downstream from the plant was improved, leading to an increase in the number of anglers fishing for bass. · (D) Because of the new plant, the level of noise downstream increased, making that section of the river a less popular place for anglers to fish. · (E) The discharged wastewater created turbulence that disrupted the vegetation of the river downstream, destroying some of the bass's natural habitat.\n\nA 1% · B 1% · C 65% · D 30% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that ...**\nThe power plant opened and started discharging wastewater into the river.\n\n**Why is it that ...**\nShortly after, anglers downstream caught fewer bass overall?\n\n**Evaluate**\nThis isn't a true paradox. Nothing here is surprising. The stem just wants explanations for a drop in the number of bass caught.\n\nThink about what \"number of bass caught\" depends on. It takes two things: bass in the water and people fishing for them. So there are two roads to fewer bass caught:\n1. **Fewer bass downstream.** They died, got eaten, moved away, or lost their habitat.\n2. **Less fishing downstream.** Fewer anglers, or anglers fishing less.\n\nUsually, on EXCEPT questions, three of the four answers we eliminate come at the stimulus from one angle, and the fourth takes a different tactic. Here, expect three answers on road 1 and one sneaking in on road 2.\n\nMost students only think of road 1, because the wastewater feels like it must be hurting the fish. But road 2 is just as good. If half the anglers stop showing up, half as many bass get caught, even if the bass are thriving.\n\n**Goal**\nEliminate four answers that explain fewer bass caught, by either road. The correct answer will do neither, or it will push the other way: more bass or more fishing, which should mean *more* bass caught.\n\nBe careful with any answer about anglers. It isn't out of scope. Anglers are half the equation.\n\n---\n\n## 7. PT156-S4-Q10 · Paradox EXCEPT · Difficulty 5 · Answer D\n\n*Not loaded yet. The bank labels this Most Strongly Supported; it's a Paradox EXCEPT. Modelled on PT112-S4-Q5 and PT106-S2-Q26 (golden set: hard Paradox EXCEPT), with the worked numbers from PT111-S4-Q4.*\n\n> While the population of city X is approximately one-half that of city Y, the number of city X residents who are patients in hospitals is only one-fourth that of the number of city Y residents who are patients in hospitals.\n>\n> Each of the following, if true, contributes to an explanation of the difference in the number of residents who are patients in hospitals except:\n>\n> (A) Preventive health programs are more prevalent in city X than in city Y. · (B) The hospitals in city X are noted as leaders in employing outpatient treatment wherever possible. · (C) The drinking water of city Y has dangerously high levels of pollutants, whereas this is not the case for city X. · (D) The hospitals in city Y are of very high quality, and residents of city X are often sent there for treatment. · (E) The lifestyle in city X is significantly less stressful than the lifestyle in city Y.\n\nA 3% · B 14% · C 4% · D 61% · E 18%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that ...**\nCity X has about half the population of city Y.\n\n**How can it be that ...**\nCity X has only a quarter as many residents in the hospital?\n\n**Evaluate**\nPut numbers on it. Say city X has 100,000 people and city Y has 200,000. If X has 100 residents in the hospital, Y has 400. That's 1 in 1,000 for X and 2 in 1,000 for Y. Per person, X residents end up in the hospital half as often.\n\nSo we need a difference between the cities that makes an X resident less likely to be a hospital patient. Two roads:\n1. **X residents are healthier.** Less disease, cleaner water, better prevention, less stress.\n2. **Sick X residents are less likely to be *admitted*.** They get treated some other way, so they never count as \"patients in hospitals.\"\n\nNow the detail the whole question turns on: the stat counts *residents* of each city who are patients in hospitals. It doesn't say which city's hospitals. An X resident in a hospital in city Y is still an X resident who's a hospital patient.\n\n**Goal**\nEliminate four answers that give X residents a reason to be healthier or less likely to be admitted. The exception will explain something else, most likely which *hospitals* are busy rather than which city's *residents* are in them.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Helps Explain.**\nOur job here: given that X has half of Y's population, why does it have only a quarter of Y's hospital patients?\n\nThis answer says, \"Fewer X residents are in the hospital because more of them are in preventive programs, so fewer get sick enough to need one.\" Road 1.\n\n**(B) Helps Explain.**\nThis answer says, \"Fewer X residents are in the hospital because X's hospitals treat people as outpatients whenever they can.\" Outpatients go home the same day. They're never admitted, so they never count as patients in the hospital. Road 2.\n\nThis is tempting because it sounds like a compliment to X's hospitals rather than an explanation. But remember what's being counted: residents *who are patients in hospitals*. Outpatient care keeps people out of that count.\n\n**(C) Helps Explain.**\nThis answer says, \"More Y residents are in the hospital because Y's water is polluted and makes people sick.\" The paradox is about the *ratio* between the cities, so a reason Y is worse off works just as well as a reason X is better off.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nThis answer says, \"X residents are often sent to Y's hospitals.\" But where they're treated doesn't change who they are. An X resident in a Y hospital is still an X resident who is a patient in a hospital.\n\nSo (D) explains why Y's *hospitals* might be crowded. It does nothing to explain why fewer *X residents* are hospital patients. If anything, being sent somewhere for treatment means X residents *are* being hospitalized, which pushes the other way.\n\nHard EXCEPT questions often hinge on one precise word in the stimulus. Here it was \"residents.\" When you're stuck between two answers, go back and ask exactly what's being counted.\n\n**(E) Helps Explain.**\nThis was the most popular wrong answer, probably because stress feels like a weak, indirect reason. But the stem only asks what \"contributes to an explanation,\" which is a low bar. Less stress means fewer stress-related illnesses (heart trouble, for one), which means fewer X residents in the hospital. It doesn't have to explain the whole gap. It just has to help.\n\n---\n\n## 8. PT110-S2-Q8 · Method · Difficulty 2 · Answer A\n\n*Modelled on PT144-S2-Q8 (golden set: two-speaker Method, \"the respondent never denies the evidence\") and PT147-S4-Q12 (numbers inside the evidence).*\n\n> Conservationist: The risk to airplane passengers from collisions between airplanes using the airport and birds from the wildlife refuge is negligible. In the 10 years since the refuge was established, only 20 planes have been damaged in collisions with birds, and no passenger has been injured as a result of such a collision. The wildlife refuge therefore poses no safety risk.\n>\n> Pilot: You neglect to mention that 17 of those 20 collisions occurred within the past 2 years, and that the number of birds in the refuge is rapidly increasing. As the number of collisions between birds and airplanes increases, so does the likelihood that at least one such collision will result in passenger injuries.\n>\n> The pilot counters the conservationist by\n>\n> (A) attempting to show that the conservationist's description of the facts is misleading · (B) questioning the conservationist's motives for reaching a certain conclusion · (C) asserting that dangerous situations inevitably become more dangerous with the passage of time · (D) discrediting the moral principle on which the conservationist's argument is based · (E) disputing the accuracy of the figures cited by the conservationist\n\nA 85% · B 0% · C 10% · D 0% · E 5%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conservationist's Conclusion (therefore)**\nThe wildlife refuge poses no safety risk to airplane passengers.\n\n**Conservationist's Evidence**\nIn 10 years, only 20 planes have been damaged by birds from the refuge, and no passenger has been hurt.\n\n**Pilot's Response**\n17 of those 20 collisions happened in the last 2 years, and the bird population is growing fast. More collisions means a higher chance one of them hurts a passenger.\n\n**Evaluate**\nFirst question on any two-speaker Method: was the second person adding to the first person's argument or pushing back? Pushing back, clearly. So next: pushing back on what?\n\nNotice what the pilot does *not* say. He doesn't say \"it wasn't 20 collisions\" or \"someone actually got hurt.\" He accepts every number the conservationist gave.\n\nWhat he attacks is the picture those numbers paint. \"20 collisions in 10 years\" sounds like 2 a year, steady and harmless. But 17 of them happened in the last 2 years, so the real rate is about 8 a year and climbing. The 10-year average hides a trend.\n\nThis is the most common way a second speaker pushes back on the LSAT. They almost never deny the first speaker's evidence. They accept it and add a fact that changes what it means.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for something like: \"The pilot accepts the conservationist's facts but argues they were presented in a way that gives the wrong impression.\"\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\n\"Misleading\" is the right word. The conservationist's facts are accurate, but her description (20 over 10 years, no injuries) leaves out the timing that makes the refuge look safe. The pilot supplies the missing piece to show the risk is growing fast.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.**\nThe pilot never suggests the conservationist has a hidden agenda. He doesn't say \"you just want to protect the birds.\" He argues with her reasoning, not her motives.\n\n**(C) Bad Description.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer, for students who notice the pilot is talking about the future. But the pilot's point is specific: collisions are rising *because* the bird population is rising. He never says dangerous situations *inevitably* get worse with the passage of time. Time isn't the cause in his argument. More birds is. And \"dangerous situations\" in general is far broader than this one airport.\n\n**(D) Bad Description.**\nThere's no moral principle in the conservationist's argument. Safety risk is a factual question. There's nothing for the pilot to discredit.\n\n**(E) Bad Description.**\nIn almost every Method of Response question, one answer says the second speaker disputes or denies the first speaker's evidence. It's almost never right, and it isn't here. The pilot doesn't dispute the figures. He relies on them: \"17 of *those* 20 collisions\" only works if the 20 is accurate.\n\n---\n\n## 9. PT117-S3-Q8 · Method · Difficulty 3 · Answer A\n\n*Choice Notes only. This question already has an Argument Breakdown, which stays as it is. The bank labels it Weaken; the stem asks how Rossi's argument proceeds, so it's Method. Modelled on PT118-S1-Q7 (Abstract Answers + Plans / Recommendations) and PT139-S1-Q23.*\n\n> Rossi: It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented. So children should have the right to vote, since sometimes the interests of children are different from those of their parents.\n>\n> Smith: Granted, children's interests are not always the same as their parents'; governmental deficits incurred by their parents' generation will later affect their own generation's standard of living. But even if children are told about the issues affecting them, which is not generally the case, their conceptions of what can or should be done are too simple, and their time horizons are radically different from those of adults, so we cannot give them the responsibility of voting.\n>\n> Which one of the following most accurately describes Rossi's argument?\n>\n> (A) It makes an appeal to a general principle. · (B) It denies the good faith of an opponent. · (C) It relies on evaluating the predictable consequences of a proposal. · (D) It substitutes description for giving a rationale for a policy. · (E) It employs a term on two different occasions in different senses.\n\nA 78% · B 1% · C 6% · D 11% · E 4%\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\nRossi's first sentence is a general rule: it's undemocratic for *anyone* to live under a government that doesn't represent their interests. Then he applies it to one group. Children's interests sometimes differ from their parents', so, by the rule, children need their own representation, which means the vote.\n\n\"Appeal to a general principle\" is how the LSAT describes this move. Whenever an argument opens with a broad \"it is wrong / undemocratic / unfair to ...\" and then applies it to a specific case, this answer is in play.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.**\nRossi speaks first. He has no opponent yet, and he never questions anyone's honesty. (Smith doesn't do this either.)\n\n**(C) Bad Description.**\nRossi's argument is about what's *democratic*, not what would happen if children voted. He never predicts any results. If anyone weighs practical consequences, it's Smith, who worries children's views are too simple for the responsibility. That's probably why this answer feels familiar: it describes the other speaker.\n\n**(D) Bad Description.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer, maybe because Rossi's argument is short and sounds like he's just stating things. But he does give a rationale. The policy is \"children should vote.\" The rationale is the principle (unrepresented interests are undemocratic) plus the fact (children's interests sometimes differ). That's a reason, not a description.\n\n**(E) Bad Description.**\nThis is the famous Equivocation flaw. The only term Rossi uses twice is \"interests,\" and it means the same thing both times: what's good for a person. No shift in meaning.\n\n---\n\n## 10. PT112-S1-Q3 · Necessary Assumption · Difficulty 3 · Answer C\n\n*Modelled on PT137-S3-Q11 (golden set: all four features shared, \"solve the riddle\" Evaluate) and PT122-S1-Q10 (Defender).*\n\n> Finnish author Jaakko Mikkeli was accused by Norwegian author Kirsten Halden of plagiarizing a book that she had written and that had been published 20 years before Mikkeli's. The two books, although set in different periods and regions, contain enough plot similarities to make coincidental resemblance unlikely. Mikkeli's defense rests on his argument that plagiarism was impossible in this case because Halden's book has been published only in Norwegian, a language Mikkeli does not understand, and because no reviews of Halden's book have ever been published.\n>\n> The argument in Mikkeli's defense depends on the assumption that\n>\n> (A) Mikkeli has never met Halden · (B) Halden's book did not become popular in Norway · (C) nobody related the plot of Halden's book in detail to Mikkeli before Mikkeli wrote his book · (D) there is a common European myth to which both authors referred subconsciously in the books in question · (E) Mikkeli is not familiar with Old Icelandic, an extinct language related to an earlier form of Norwegian\n\nA 1% · B 6% · C 80% · D 1% · E 12%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nPlagiarism was impossible in this case.\n\n**Evidence (because)**\n- Halden's book has only been published in Norwegian, which Mikkeli can't read.\n- No reviews of Halden's book have ever been published.\n\n**Evaluate**\nMikkeli's defense is: I had no way to know what was in that book. He's closed two doors. He couldn't read it, and he couldn't read a review of it.\n\nTo find the wiggle room, solve this riddle:\n  *Given that ...* he can't read Norwegian and there are no reviews,\n  *How could we argue that ...* he still could have plagiarized it?\n\nWhat other doors are there?\n  - Someone who reads Norwegian could have told him the plot.\n  - An unpublished translation could have been passed around.\n  - There could have been a film, a radio play, or a talk about the book.\n\n\"Impossible\" is a strong word. To claim plagiarism was impossible, Mikkeli needs every door shut, not just the two he mentions.\n\n**Goal**\nThe correct answer will most likely be a defender: it rules out one of the other doors, like \"no one told Mikkeli the plot.\" Negate it and we should get a way for Mikkeli to have learned the story.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Out of Scope.**\nNegate it: Mikkeli *has* met Halden. So what? Shaking her hand at a conference doesn't mean she told him the plot of her book. (If she did, that's the scenario in (C).) The negation doesn't give him access to the story.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nNegate it: the book *was* popular in Norway. That still doesn't get the story to a Finnish author who can't read Norwegian. Popularity might make it more likely someone talked about the book, but \"someone told him\" is (C)'s idea, not this one.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\nNegate it: someone *did* tell Mikkeli the plot in detail before he wrote his book. Now plagiarism is very possible. He didn't need to read Norwegian or find a review. He just needed a friend who'd read it.\n\nThis is a defender. It protects the argument from an objection rather than linking the evidence to the conclusion. When an argument says something was *impossible*, look for the answer that rules out one more way it could have happened. And notice the ruling-out word, \"nobody.\" Remove it and the objection appears.\n\n**(D) Opposite.**\nA common myth would *help* Mikkeli by explaining the similarities innocently. But his defense doesn't depend on it; his argument is about access. Negate (D), so there's no common myth, and his \"I had no access\" argument is exactly as strong as before.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.**\nThis is the most tempting wrong answer, because it sounds like another language door. But Old Icelandic is extinct and only related to an *earlier* form of Norwegian. Negate it, so Mikkeli knows Old Icelandic, and he still can't read modern Norwegian. Halden's book came out 20 years before his, not 800. Knowing an ancient cousin of the language doesn't let him read the book.\n\n---\n\n## 11. PT114-S2-Q21 · Necessary Assumption · Difficulty 4 · Answer C\n\n*Modelled on PT118-S3-Q19 (all four features shared: Argue the Anti-Conclusion, Defender, Net Effect, Plans / Recommendations) and PT104-S4-Q4.*\n\n> So-called \"engineered foods,\" usually in powder or liquid form, consist of protein that is distilled from natural sources and supplemented with vitamins and minerals. Although the amino acids contained in such products stimulate the production of growth hormones, these hormones produce growth in connective tissue rather than in muscle mass; this does not improve muscle strength. Hence, athletes, who need to improve their muscular strength, should not consume engineered foods.\n>\n> The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?\n>\n> (A) An increase in muscle mass produces an increase in strength. · (B) People who are not athletes require neither stronger connective tissue nor muscle strength. · (C) If an engineered food does not improve muscle strength, there is no other substantial advantage to athletes from consuming it. · (D) Consuming engineered foods that provide nutrients that can be obtained more easily elsewhere is unhealthy. · (E) Growth of muscle mass enhances muscle strength only when accompanied by growth of connective tissue.\n\nA 26% · B 0% · C 71% · D 1% · E 2%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (hence)**\nAthletes should not consume engineered foods.\n\n**Evidence**\n  - Engineered foods are protein plus vitamins and minerals.\n  - Their amino acids stimulate growth hormones, but those hormones grow connective tissue, not muscle mass.\n  - That doesn't improve muscle strength.\n  - Athletes need to improve their muscle strength.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThe evidence shows engineered foods won't do one thing: build muscle strength. The conclusion says athletes shouldn't eat them at all.\n\nWhenever an author's conclusion is a recommendation, she's implicitly saying \"the world where you follow my advice is better, on the whole, than the world where you don't.\" That's a Net Effect claim. Showing that one benefit is missing doesn't prove the plan is a net loss.\n\n  *Given that ...* engineered foods don't improve muscle strength,\n  *How could we argue that ...* athletes should still consume them?\n  - They're protein with vitamins and minerals. Maybe they help with recovery, energy, or basic nutrition.\n  - Stronger connective tissue sounds like it could prevent injuries. Plenty of athletes would sign up for that.\n  - Maybe they're just a convenient way to get calories during a heavy training block.\n\nAny real benefit could make them worth eating, even if they don't build strength.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for a defender: an answer that rules out any other substantial benefit to athletes. Negate it and we should get \"engineered foods do offer athletes something else worthwhile,\" which kills the \"should not consume\" conclusion.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Reversal.**\nThis is the big trap, and it feels necessary because it seems to be the logic hiding inside the premise. But look at what the author actually *says*: the hormones grow connective tissue rather than muscle, and \"this does not improve muscle strength.\" She asserts the no-strength result directly. The argument doesn't need a separate rule about muscle mass to get there.\n\nRun the negation test: an increase in muscle mass does *not* produce an increase in strength. Does that make engineered foods better for athletes? No. They still don't grow muscle, and they still don't improve strength. The argument is untouched.\n\nThe gap on this question is between the evidence and the conclusion (no strength benefit → don't eat them), not inside the evidence. An answer that just props up a premise is sometimes called a Premise Booster, and it's almost never the necessary assumption.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nThe argument is only about athletes. Negate (B), so some non-athletes do need stronger connective tissue, and the argument about athletes is unaffected.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\nNegate it: even if an engineered food doesn't improve strength, athletes *do* get some other substantial advantage from it. Now \"athletes should not consume engineered foods\" falls apart. Maybe they should eat them for that other advantage.\n\nThis is the defender we predicted. Whenever the conclusion is a recommendation (should / should not), check whether the author weighed *all* the effects or just one.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.**\nThe argument never says engineered foods are unhealthy, or that their nutrients are easier to get elsewhere. Negate (D), so these foods are perfectly healthy, and the author's only reason (no strength benefit) still stands.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.**\nThis is about how muscle growth and connective tissue work together. The argument never relies on it. Negate it (muscle growth can boost strength even without connective tissue growth) and nothing changes, because engineered foods don't produce muscle growth in the first place.\n\n---\n\n## 12. PT114-S4-Q12 · Sufficient Assumption · Difficulty 2 · Answer E\n\n*Modelled on PT113-S4-Q20 (diagram each answer, \"does the trigger apply?\") and PT146-S2-Q3 (golden set: New Concept in Conclusion, contrapositive as the correct form).*\n\n> Morris: Computers, despite some people's expectations, will have an inappreciable impact on education. To be sure, computers are useful for drills promoting memorization, though only a small part of education can be accomplished through drills. But machines cannot help students with any of the higher intellectual functions we call understanding; for that, human teachers are indispensable.\n>\n> The conclusion of Morris's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?\n>\n> (A) Whatever memorization is necessary can be accomplished as easily without computers as with them. · (B) Requiring memorization in appreciable amounts tends to thwart development of higher intellectual functions in students. · (C) Successful memorization of relevant facts is a necessary precondition for the development of higher intellectual functions in students. · (D) Many students become familiar with computers before encountering them at school. · (E) Having an appreciable impact on education involves affecting the higher intellectual functions of students.\n\nA 5% · B 5% · C 7% · D 0% · E 83%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nComputers will have an inappreciable impact on education.\n\n**Evidence**\n  - Computers help with memorization drills, but drills are only a small part of education.\n  - Computers can't help with the higher intellectual functions (understanding). Only human teachers can.\n\n**Evaluate**\nMorris's conclusion has a New Concept the evidence never mentions: an \"appreciable impact on education.\" The evidence talks about drills and higher intellectual functions, but nothing says what it takes to have an appreciable impact.\n\nSo we need a bridge from what the evidence says about computers to the new concept:\n```\ncan't help with higher    →   inappreciable impact\nintellectual functions        on education\n```\nOr its contrapositive, which is an equally good correct answer:\n```\nappreciable impact    →   helps with higher\non education              intellectual functions\n```\nEither version finishes the job. If an appreciable impact requires touching the higher functions, and computers can't touch them, computers can't have an appreciable impact.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer that connects \"appreciable impact on education\" to the higher intellectual functions, most likely as a requirement: an appreciable impact needs to affect students' understanding.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Weak.**\nThis closes one door: computers don't even add anything to memorization. But it doesn't close all of them. Could computers still have an appreciable impact on education some other way (organizing information, motivating students, connecting students to teachers)? Nothing in (A) rules that out. Morris needs a rule that says the *only* road to an appreciable impact runs through the higher functions. (A) doesn't give us that.\n\n**(B) Weakens.**\nIf lots of memorization actually *hurts* the development of higher functions, and computers push memorization, then computers might have a big (bad) impact on education. That's an appreciable impact, which works against Morris.\n\n**(C) Weakens.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer. If memorization is a necessary step toward higher functions, then computers, which help with memorization, might be helping indirectly with understanding after all. That opens a door to computers having an appreciable impact. Morris wants that door shut.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.**\nWhen students first meet computers says nothing about the size of computers' impact on their education.\n\n**(E) Correct.**\nThis is the contrapositive version of our bridge:\n```\nappreciable impact    →   affects higher\non education              intellectual functions\n```\nDoes the trigger apply? Take the contrapositive: if computers don't affect the higher functions, they don't have an appreciable impact. The evidence says computers can't help with those functions. So computers can't have an appreciable impact. The conclusion is proven.\n\nOn Sufficient Assumption, when the conclusion has a concept the evidence never mentions, the right answer almost always defines that new concept in terms of something the evidence did cover.\n\n---\n\n## 13. PT105-S1-Q3 · Strengthen · Difficulty 1 · Answer C\n\n*Modelled on PT127-S1-Q23 (Assumes Difference + Plans / Recommendations: \"establishing a difference the author is assuming\") and PT115-S2-Q10.*\n\n> Space programs have recently suffered several setbacks with respect to their large projects, and much money has been lost. Consequently, these grand projects should be abandoned in favor of several small ones.\n>\n> Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the reasoning above?\n>\n> (A) The cost of starting a space project increases every year. · (B) It is just as easy to revise, and even scrap, small projects as it is large ones. · (C) Large projects are intrinsically more likely to fail and so are more financially risky than small projects. · (D) Project managers prefer to work on small projects rather than large ones. · (E) Large space projects can explore a few places thoroughly, while small projects can investigate more regions, though less thoroughly.\n\nA 1% · B 2% · C 96% · D 1% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (consequently)**\nSpace programs should drop their large projects in favor of several small ones.\n\n**Evidence**\nLarge space projects have had several recent setbacks, and a lot of money has been lost.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThe author recommends a switch: large projects out, small projects in. The only evidence is that large projects have been going badly.\n\nHow would an opponent push back?\n  *Given that ...* large projects have lost a lot of money,\n  *How could we argue that ...* we still shouldn't switch to small ones?\n  - Maybe small projects would lose just as much, or fail just as often.\n  - Maybe the recent setbacks were bad luck, not something about being large.\n\nThe author is assuming there's a meaningful difference between large and small projects: that the size is the problem, and small ones would do better.\n\n**Goal**\nTo strengthen, we can establish the difference the author is assuming: large projects, because they're large, are more likely to fail or waste money than small ones.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.**\nRising start-up costs hit *every* space project, large or small, so this doesn't give us a reason to prefer one over the other. (If anything, launching *several* small projects means paying that rising start-up cost several times.)\n\n**(B) Weakens.**\nIf small projects are no easier to revise or scrap than large ones, that removes one possible advantage of going small. It pulls the two options closer together, which hurts an argument that says one is better.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\nThis is the difference the author was assuming. Large projects are *intrinsically* more likely to fail, so they're riskier with money. Now the recent setbacks aren't bad luck; they're what you'd expect from large projects, and small ones would be safer.\n\nWhenever an argument recommends switching from one option to another, the best strengtheners show the new option is actually better on the exact thing the evidence complained about. Here, that's failure and lost money.\n\n**(D) No Impact.**\nWhat project managers like to work on doesn't tell us which projects succeed or lose money. The argument is about setbacks and money, not job satisfaction.\n\n**(E) Unclear Impact.**\nThis is a trade-off: large projects go deep, small ones go wide. It doesn't say either approach avoids setbacks or saves money, and it doesn't say which is better. We can't tell whether it makes the switch look good or bad.\n\n---\n\n## 14. PT120-S4-Q9 · Principle-Strengthen · Difficulty 2 · Answer C\n\n*Modelled on PT146-S1-Q1 (every principle diagrammed, then \"does the trigger apply?\") and PT148-S1-Q4.*\n\n> Writer: I collaborated with another writer on my last book, instead of writing alone as I usually do. Because the book sold so well as a result of this joint effort, I should collaborate with a writer on my next book so that book will sell well too.\n>\n> Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?\n>\n> (A) If a person's book sells well because of a collaboration, that person's next book will sell well, if he or she collaborates with the same writer. · (B) A book sells well only if its author collaborated on the book with another writer. · (C) If a person's book sells well because of a collaboration, future collaborations on the part of that person will produce other books that sell well. · (D) Writers who do not collaborate on books have a smaller chance of writing a book that will sell well. · (E) Writers who collaborate on books, if they are good writers, usually produce books that sell well.\n\nA 5% · B 7% · C 84% · D 2% · E 2%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (should = opinion)**\nI should collaborate with a writer on my next book, so it will sell well too.\n\n**Evidence (because)**\nMy last book was a collaboration, and it sold well *because of* that collaboration.\n\n**Evaluate**\nOn Principle-Strengthen, we prephrase a rule that sounds like \"If premise, then conclusion.\" So in this case:\n```\nmy book sold well    →   collaborating again will\nbecause of a             make my next book sell\ncollaboration            well (so I should)\n```\nNotice the conclusion says collaborate with *a* writer, not the same writer. Our principle has to cover any collaboration.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for a rule whose trigger matches our evidence (a book sold well because of a collaboration) and whose outcome delivers our conclusion (future collaborations will produce books that sell well).\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Conclusion Match.**\nThis rule would look like this:\n```\nbook sold well because    →   next book sells well\nof a collaboration            IF same co-writer\n```\nThe trigger applies. But the outcome only promises success with *the same* co-writer. The writer's conclusion is to collaborate with \"a writer,\" any writer. (A) says nothing about a new partner, so it can't justify the conclusion as written.\n\n**(B) Bad Conclusion Match.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer. Diagrammed:\n```\nbook sells well    →   author collaborated\n```\nSo yes, if the writer wants the next book to sell well, he'd better collaborate. But the conclusion also promises that collaborating means the book \"*will* sell well.\" (B) never promises that. It only says you can't sell well *without* collaboration. Collaboration could be required and still not be enough.\n\n(B) also ignores the writer's evidence completely. His reasoning is \"collaboration *caused* my last book's success.\" (B) would make that evidence pointless.\n\n**(C) Correct.**\n```\nbook sold well because    →   future collaborations\nof a collaboration            produce books that sell well\n```\nDoes the trigger apply? Yes: his last book sold well because of the collaboration. Does the outcome deliver the conclusion? Yes: if he collaborates on the next book, it will sell well. Both halves match, word for word.\n\n**(D) Too Weak.**\nA \"smaller chance\" of selling well without collaboration doesn't mean collaboration will make the next book sell well. It only compares odds. The writer's conclusion is confident: the next book *will* sell well.\n\n**(E) Bad Trigger Match.**\n```\nwriter collaborates + is    →   usually produces\na good writer                    books that sell well\n```\nDoes the trigger apply? We don't know whether our writer is a good writer. And \"usually\" is weaker than the writer's conclusion. Two strikes.\n\n---\n\n## 15. PT105-S4-Q12 · Principle-Conform · Difficulty 2 · Answer A\n\n*Modelled on PT107-S1-Q19 (Important Pivot + Principles in Answers) and PT135-S1-Q6 (golden set: boil the stimulus down to a slogan).*\n\n> Nearly everyone has complained of a mistaken utility bill that cannot easily be corrected or of computer files that cannot readily be retrieved. Yet few people today would tolerate waiting in long lines while clerks search for information that can now be found in seconds, and almost no one who has used a word processor would return to a typewriter.\n>\n> The information above conforms most closely to which one of the following principles?\n>\n> (A) The fact that people complain about some consequences of technology cannot be taken as a reliable indication that they would choose to live without it. · (B) If people do not complain about some technology, then it is probably not a significant factor in their daily lives. · (C) The degree to which technologies elicit complaints from people is always an accurate measure of the extent to which people have become dependent on them. · (D) The complaints people make about technological innovations are more reliable evidence of the importance of those innovations than the choices people actually make. · (E) The less willing people are to do without technology the more likely they are to complain about the effects of technology.\n\nA 84% · B 1% · C 4% · D 5% · E 5%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements**\n  - Nearly everyone has complained about some technology problem (a billing error, lost computer files).\n  - *pivot (yet)*\n  - Hardly anyone would go back to waiting in line for clerks, and almost no one would trade a word processor for a typewriter.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThere's no conclusion here. It's two observations joined by \"yet,\" and the pivot tells us they pull against each other.\n\nWhen a Principle-Conform stimulus has no explicit principle, we don't diagram. We articulate the moral of the story and look for the answer that matches it.\n\nThe tension: people complain about technology all the time, but when it comes down to it, they wouldn't give it up.\n\nSlogan: *People gripe about technology, but they wouldn't live without it.*\n\n**Goal**\nLook for a principle that says complaints about technology don't mean people would actually choose to go without it. The right answer should cover both halves: the complaints and the choice to keep the technology.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.**\nThis is our slogan in formal clothes:\n- \"people complain about some consequences of technology\": billing errors and lost files.\n- \"cannot be taken as a reliable indication that they would choose to live without it\": nobody's going back to typewriters.\n\nOn Conform questions with no conclusion, boil the stimulus down to one sentence first. The right principle is usually easy to spot after that.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.**\nThe stimulus is only about technology people *do* complain about. It says nothing about technology no one complains about, so it can't illustrate a rule about that group.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.**\n\"Always an accurate measure\" is extreme. And the stimulus actually points the other way: complaints *don't* tell you how attached people really are. Everyone complains, and their choices show they depend on it anyway.\n\n**(D) Opposite.**\nThe stimulus suggests people's choices (keeping the word processor) tell you more than their complaints. (D) says complaints are the better evidence.\n\n**(E) Unsupported Relationship.**\nThis is a sliding scale: the more you depend on technology, the more you complain. The stimulus never compares degrees. Nearly everyone complains and nearly everyone would keep the technology. Nothing about more of one producing more of the other.\n\n---\n\n## 16. PT116-S2-Q19 · Agree · Difficulty 3 · Answer D\n\n*Modelled on PT154-S2-Q25 (one step per claim of the first speaker, \"Does Cortez argue ...?\") and PT145-S4-Q2 (golden set: Agree/Disagree claim table).*\n\n> Marc: The fact that the people of our country look back on the past with a great deal of nostalgia demonstrates that they regret the recent revolution.\n>\n> Robert: They are not nostalgic for the recent past, but for the distant past, which the prerevolutionary regime despised; this indicates that although they are troubled, they do not regret the revolution.\n>\n> Their dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Marc and Robert agree that the people of their country\n>\n> (A) tend to underrate past problems when the country faces troubling times · (B) are looking to the past for solutions to the country's current problems · (C) are likely to repeat former mistakes if they look to the country's past for solutions to current problems · (D) are concerned about the country's current situation and this is evidenced by their nostalgia · (E) tend to be most nostalgic for the things that are the farthest in their past\n\nA 5% · B 8% · C 1% · D 77% · E 9%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Marc's 1st Claim**\nThe people look back on the past with a great deal of nostalgia.\n\nDoes Robert agree? **Yes.** He says they're nostalgic for the *distant* past rather than the recent past. He's correcting *what* they're nostalgic for, not *whether* they're nostalgic.\n\n**Marc's 2nd Claim**\nThat nostalgia shows the people regret the recent revolution.\n\nDoes Robert agree? **No.** That's his whole point: the nostalgia shows they're troubled, but they don't regret the revolution.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThis is an Agree question, so we're hunting for common ground, not the fight. We've got one explicit match (they're nostalgic). Now check what each speaker *reads into* the nostalgia:\n  - Marc: it shows they regret the revolution. You don't regret something unless you're unhappy with where it's left you.\n  - Robert: it shows \"they are troubled.\"\n\nSo beneath the disagreement, they share a starting point: the nostalgia is a sign that something about the present is bothering people. They only split on what that something is.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer saying the people are unhappy or concerned about their present situation, and that their nostalgia shows it. Stay away from anything only one speaker holds: regret over the revolution (Marc) or the distant past (Robert).\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Support from Either.**\nNeither speaker says the people underrate past problems. Robert notes they're nostalgic for a past the old regime despised, but that's not the same as forgetting that era's problems.\n\n**(B) No Support from Either.**\nNeither speaker mentions solutions. Nostalgia is longing for the past, not using the past to fix the present.\n\n**(C) No Support from Either.**\nSame problem as (B), and worse: nobody says anything about repeating mistakes.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nCheck both speakers:\n  - **Robert:** says the nostalgia \"indicates that ... they are troubled.\" Concerned about the present, evidenced by the nostalgia. Yes.\n  - **Marc:** says the nostalgia demonstrates they regret the recent revolution. Regretting the revolution means being unhappy with what it's brought, which is the country's current situation. Yes.\n\nThey disagree about *why* the people are troubled. They agree *that* they are, and that the nostalgia shows it.\n\n**(E) Half Scope.**\nThis is the most tempting wrong answer, because Robert does say the people are nostalgic for the distant past. But Marc never says which part of the past. And \"*most* nostalgic for the things *farthest* back\" is a ranking neither of them makes. Robert only says distant rather than recent, not that nostalgia grows the farther back you go.\n\n---\n\n## 17. PT128-S3-Q16 · Main Conclusion · Difficulty 2 · Answer D\n\n*Not loaded yet. Modelled on PT152-S2-Q10 (conclusion in the final sentence, \"therefore\" ordering, Support Test) and PT139-S4-Q1 (golden set: swap referential language for specifics).*\n\n> The primary task of a university is to educate. But to teach well, professors must be informed about new developments in their disciplines, and that requires research. Yet many universities cannot afford to support faculty research adequately. So a lack of funds for research adversely affects the degree to which a university can fulfill its central mission.\n>\n> Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion of the argument?\n>\n> (A) In order to be able to teach well, university professors must conduct research. · (B) Lack of financial support for faculty research is the root of ineffective teaching at universities. · (C) Effective teaching is the primary mission of a university. · (D) Lack of funds for research reduces the quality of education a university provides. · (E) New means of funding faculty research at universities are needed.\n\nA 4% · B 7% · C 3% · D 85% · E 1%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (so)**\nA lack of funds for research adversely affects the degree to which a university can fulfill its central mission.\n  *rephrase:* A lack of research funding hurts how well a university can educate.\n\n**Evidence**\n  - A university's primary task is to educate.\n  - To teach well, professors have to keep up with new developments, which requires research.\n  - Many universities can't afford to support research adequately.\n\n**Evaluate**\nWhenever we do a Main Conclusion question, we remind ourselves: the conclusion is the final claim only about 10% of the time. It usually sits in the first sentence or right after a pivot. So a final \"So ...\" sentence deserves a second look before we trust it.\n\nHere, it holds up. Run the Support Test: *why should we believe a lack of research funding hurts a university's central mission?* Because the mission is to educate, teaching well requires research, and many universities can't fund research. Every earlier sentence feeds into the last one, and nothing comes after it. This is one of the 10%.\n\nAlso notice the referential language. \"Its central mission\" only makes sense if we go back to the first sentence: the mission is to educate.\n\n**Goal**\nSwap the reference for the specific idea, then look for the closest match: *a lack of research funding hurts how well a university can educate.*\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Premise.**\nThis restates the second sentence: teaching well requires keeping up, which requires research. Ask \"why should we believe this?\" and the argument doesn't say. It's support for the conclusion, not the conclusion.\n\n**(B) Too Strong.**\n\"The root of ineffective teaching\" makes lack of funding *the* cause of bad teaching. The author only says it *adversely affects* education, which leaves room for plenty of other causes.\n\n**(C) Premise.**\nThis is the first sentence, reworded (and nudged from \"educate\" to \"effective teaching\"). It's there to tell us what \"central mission\" means. It supports the conclusion; it isn't it.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nLine it up:\n- \"Lack of funds for research\": a lack of funds for research.\n- \"reduces the quality of education a university provides\": adversely affects how well a university fulfills its central mission (educating).\n\nThe only work required is swapping \"central mission\" for \"education,\" which is exactly what the Goal step set up.\n\n**(E) Unstated.**\nThe author never proposes a fix. She only says underfunding hurts education. Calling for new funding sources is a What Next answer: something the author might say next, but didn't.\n\n---\n\n## 18. PT105-S1-Q11 · Role · Difficulty 3 · Answer E\n\n*Modelled on PT107-S4-Q2 (First Sentence Conclusion, Support Test) and PT144-S3-Q17.*\n\n> Although the concept of free will is essential to that of moral responsibility, its role in determining responsibility is not the same in all situations. We hold criminals morally responsible for the damage they cause, assuming that they freely chose their activities. But we do not hold someone who has a heart attack while driving morally responsible for the damage caused, if any, even when we have good reason to believe that the heart attack could have been prevented by eating different foods and that one's choice of diet is made freely.\n>\n> The claim that a choice of diet can affect whether or not one has a heart attack plays which one of the following roles in the argument?\n>\n> (A) It is a subsidiary conclusion of the argument. · (B) It is used to show that we should hold someone morally responsible for damages caused by having a heart attack while driving. · (C) It is cited as evidence that our concept of moral responsibility should be the same in all situations. · (D) It is used to disprove the claim that we should not hold criminals morally responsible for damages. · (E) It is used in support of the conclusion of the argument.\n\nA 6% · B 3% · C 11% · D 3% · E 77%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nFree will is essential to moral responsibility, but its role in determining responsibility isn't the same in every situation.\n\n**Evidence**\n  - Criminals: we hold them responsible, because they freely chose what they did.\n  - Heart-attack drivers: we *don't* hold them responsible, even when a freely chosen diet could have prevented the heart attack.\n\n**Evaluate**\nAny time we read an argument on Role or Main Conclusion, we prime ourselves: most conclusions are an opinionated first sentence or come after a pivot. This one is the first sentence, after \"although.\"\n\nVerify with the Support Test: *why should we believe free will's role isn't the same in all situations?* Because criminals and heart-attack drivers both made free choices that led to damage, and we treat them differently.\n\nNow, where does the diet claim fit? It's inside the second example, and it's what makes that example work. The driver made a free choice (their diet) that led to the damage, just like a criminal. And yet we don't blame them.\n\nWithout the diet claim, the heart-attack example proves nothing. \"We don't blame people for random heart attacks\" doesn't show free will working differently, because there'd be no free choice in the picture at all. The diet claim sneaks free will into the heart-attack case so the contrast with criminals lands.\n\nIs anything offered to support the diet claim? No. The author just says we have good reason to believe it. So it's a premise, not a conclusion.\n\n**Goal**\nPrephrase one of four roles: Main Conclusion, Supports, Opposes, Neutral. This one Supports: a premise backing the main conclusion.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Role.**\nA subsidiary conclusion has to be supported by something and then support something else. Ask \"why should we believe a diet can affect heart attacks?\" The argument never says. It's given, not concluded.\n\n**(B) Opposite.**\nThe argument says we do *not* hold heart-attack drivers responsible. The diet claim helps show we don't blame them *even though* free choice was involved. (B) points it the other way.\n\n**(C) Opposite.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer, and it's the conclusion flipped. The author argues free will's role is *not* the same in all situations. The diet claim helps show the difference. (C) says it shows everything should be the same.\n\n**(D) Wrong Role.**\nThe argument never disputes that criminals should be held responsible. It agrees they should. And the diet claim is about heart attacks, not criminals.\n\n**(E) Correct.**\nThe diet claim is support. It puts a free choice into the heart-attack example, so the example can show that free choice doesn't always lead to responsibility. That supports the main conclusion.\n\nThe most common correct answer on Role is some version of \"premise.\" When the claim has nothing supporting it and it helps the conclusion, the plain answer is usually the right one.\n\n---\n\n## 19. PT115-S2-Q8 · Parallel · Difficulty 2 · Answer B\n\n*Modelled on PT152-S1-Q23 (running comparison of each answer against the recipe) and PT155-S2-Q19 (golden set: non-formal parallel, strip the topic to a story).*\n\n> The kind of thoughts that keep a person from falling asleep can arise in either half of the brain. Therefore, a person being prevented from sleeping solely by such thoughts would be able to fall asleep by closing the eyes and counting sheep, because this activity fully occupies the left half of the brain with counting and the right half of the brain with imagining sheep, thereby excluding the sleep-preventing thoughts.\n>\n> Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning in the argument above?\n>\n> (A) Stucco is a poor insulator but brick and wood are good insulators, so a person who wants to build a house in an area with a cold climate should use brick or wood instead of stucco. · (B) Cats can damage furniture with either their claws or their teeth, so such damage can be prevented by providing cats with other objects that they will claw and bite, such as toy mice. · (C) This map indicates two roads of equal length each leading to Centreville, so a person who wants to take the shortest route to Centreville could choose either one. · (D) These chemicals are harmless by themselves but explosive when mixed together, so in order to be kept in the same laboratory without risk, they should be stored separately. · (E) This island has two harbors but one of them is too shallow to permit large ships, so this ship will have to dock in the other harbor in order to unload its cargo.\n\nA 4% · B 87% · C 1% · D 6% · E 2%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (therefore)**\nCounting sheep would let a person fall asleep, if sleep-preventing thoughts are the only thing keeping them up.\n\n**Evidence**\n  - Sleep-preventing thoughts can come from either half of the brain.\n  - Counting sheep fully occupies both halves (left counts, right imagines), leaving no room for those thoughts.\n\n**Evaluate**\nThere's no conditional or quantified language to diagram, so we boil it down to a story. Strip out the brains and the sheep:\n1. A problem can come from either of two sources.\n2. One activity keeps *both* sources busy.\n3. So that activity prevents the problem.\n\n**Goal**\nWe want a conclusion saying some activity will prevent a problem, backed by two premises: the problem has two possible sources, and the activity occupies both of them.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.**\nOne material is bad, two are good, so use a good one. That's choosing between options. There's no problem with two sources, and nothing keeping those sources busy.\n\n**(B) Correct.**\nMap it:\n- Problem: damaged furniture. (Sleeplessness.)\n- Two sources: claws or teeth. (Left or right half of the brain.)\n- One activity occupying both: toys to claw *and* bite. (Counting sheep, which uses both halves.)\n- So the problem is prevented.\n\nEvery ingredient lines up, including the idea that the fix works by giving each source something else to do.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.**\nTwo equal routes, so either one works. There's no problem being blocked and nothing being occupied. The \"two\" here is two options, not two sources of trouble.\n\n**(D) Bad Premise Match.**\nThis is the most tempting wrong answer, since it also has two things and a way to prevent harm. But the recipe is different. In (D), the problem only happens when the two chemicals come *together*, and the fix is to keep them *apart*. In the original, each source can cause the problem on its own, and the fix is to keep *both* occupied. Separating vs. occupying: different recipe.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.**\nTwo harbors, one ruled out, so use the other. That's process of elimination, not blocking a problem at both of its sources.\n\n---\n\n## 20. PT104-S4-Q13 · Parallel Flaw · Difficulty 4 · Answer D\n\n*Modelled on PT106-S1-Q3 (Part vs. Whole: \"Conversationally, what is our objection?\" carried into every answer) and PT111-S3-Q6.*\n\n> Historian: The ancient Greeks failed to recognize that, morally, democracy is no improvement over monarchy. It is wrong for an individual to have the power to choose the course of action for a government, so it is no less wrong to grant this power to society, which is just a collection of individuals.\n>\n> The pattern of flawed reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?\n>\n> (A) There is no point in trying to find someone else to solve that problem. If Robin cannot solve it, then none of Robin's friends would be able to solve it. · (B) We should not pick Hank for the relay team. He has not won a race all season, so there is no reason to expect him to help the relay team win. · (C) Laws that contain exemptions for some individuals based on no relevant consideration are fundamentally immoral. If it is wrong for a given person to commit an act, then it is wrong for anyone else in similar circumstances to commit the act. · (D) There is no point in asking the club to purchase tents and make them available for use by club members. No member of the club can afford one of those tents, so the club is unable to afford any either. · (E) Agreeing with all of the other members of society does not guarantee that one is correct about an issue. With many topics it is possible for society to be mistaken and hence every individual in society to be likewise mistaken.\n\nA 5% · B 2% · C 17% · D 66% · E 10%\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion**\nMorally, democracy is no improvement over monarchy.\n\n**Intermediate Conclusion (so)**\nIt's no less wrong to give the power to run the government to society.\n\n**Evidence**\n  - It's wrong for one individual to have the power to choose the government's course.\n  - Society is just a collection of individuals.\n\n**Evaluate**\nOn Parallel Flaw, name the flaw first.\n\nConversationally, what's our objection?\n  *Given that ...* it's wrong for one individual to hold all the power,\n  *How could we argue that ...* it's fine for society as a whole to hold it?\n\nBecause groups can have properties their members don't. One person running the country might be wrong because it's one unchecked person. A whole society deciding together has debate, checks and majority votes. The very thing that made it wrong for the individual could be missing for the group.\n\nThat's the Famous Part vs. Whole flaw: what's true of each part is assumed to be true of the whole. One brick can't hold up a roof. Many bricks together can.\n\n**Goal**\nLook for an answer we can hit with the same objection: \"Sure, each member can't / shouldn't, but the group they form might.\" The direction matters: part to whole. Answers that go whole to part, or from one individual to other individuals, have a different flaw even if they feel similar.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Different Flaw.**\nCan we make our objection? \"Sure, Robin can't solve it, but Robin's friends, as a group, might\"? Not quite. The argument goes from one individual to *other* individuals, not from members to the group they form. It's flawed (why assume Robin's friends are no smarter than Robin?), but it's a different flaw.\n\n**(B) Different Flaw.**\nHank hasn't won a race, so he won't help the relay team win. That's reasoning about one person's contribution, not \"each member can't, so the team can't.\" It's also arguably reasonable: a runner who never wins probably won't help much.\n\n**(C) Valid Logic.**\nThis is the most popular wrong answer, because it talks about individuals and wrongness, just like the historian. That's the Topic Trap. Look at the direction: it goes from what's wrong for *one person* to what's wrong for *other people in similar circumstances*. Individual to individual, not individual to group. And it's a reasonable principle, not a flaw.\n\nParallel Flaw questions love a wrong answer that copies the *topic*. Match the flaw, not the vocabulary.\n\n**(D) Correct.**\nSame objection works: \"Sure, no single member can afford a tent, but the club, pooling everyone's money, might.\"\n- No individual member can afford a tent. (No individual should hold the power.)\n- So the club, a collection of members, can't afford one either. (So society, a collection of individuals, shouldn't hold it either.)\n\nSame flaw, same direction: part to whole. It fails for the same reason too. Members can pool their money, just like a society can pool its judgment.\n\n**(E) Different Flaw.**\nThis goes the other way: society might be mistaken, so every individual might be. Whole to part. That's a flaw too, but it's the mirror image of the historian's. It also only concludes that being mistaken is *possible*, which is much weaker than the historian's firm conclusion.\n"}

## assistant

The first stage is done: every complete explanation in the database is scored and sorted into 17 question types. Picking the 10 to 20 models per type is still running, split across 9 helpers.

**Done:**
- **Pulled the answer-choice data**, with student percentages and trap tags, so the scorer can check whether the most popular trap got the most attention.
- **Scored 3,640 complete explanations.** Each was sorted into its type by reading the question stem, since the stored labels are unreliable. The scorer uses the golden-set markers:
  - how much the Evaluate step actually argues
  - a Goal that names the answer
  - no one-line "this is irrelevant" notes
  - explicit tests, examples and stated rules
  - a correct-answer note that teaches the move
  - the popular trap getting the longest note

  It deducts for the formulaic em-dash style and for mocking the question.
- **Built a shortlist of the top 25 to 40 per type** (all 17 types). Each type has between 25 and 523 complete explanations to choose from.

**Running now:** 9 helpers, each reading one to three types' shortlists in full, whole explanations, not the scores. For each type they're picking 10 to 20 models across easy, medium and hard, and across the type's sub-patterns: each famous flaw on Flaw, conditional versus story-style on Parallel, and so on. Each pick gets a rubric score and the specific moves that make it a model. They're also checking every note against the actual answer text, since misquoted choices disqualify an explanation.

**Two types may come in under 10.** Only 25 Evaluate questions have complete explanations, and only 42 Must Be False, so those may have fewer than 10 true models. If so, the helpers will say how many and why, rather than padding.

When they finish, I'll spot-check their picks against the full text and compile everything into one model library. It will list the models for each type and what the best ones do for that type. The scoring script is saved in `system/scripts/lr-explanations/` for reuse.

35	
36	## 2. What the best Flaw explanations do
37	
38	- **Build the objection in the Evaluate step, not just the label.** The best ones run "Given that ... how could we still argue that ..." and produce a concrete counter-story before the choices: the base-rate Civic (PT120-S3-Q8), and "990 present now, 980 after the firing" (PT120-S4-Q23). The famous-flaw label comes after the objection, not in place of it.
39	- **The Goal gives two acceptable shapes: formal and conversational.** "Look for the formal answer, saying this author scrambled a condition that is Sufficient ... Or look for the conversational answer saying, 'That's one possible reason'" (PT151-S4-Q23; also PT113-S2-Q3, PT154-S1-Q9). On causal arguments the two shapes are "infers causation from correlation" or "fails to consider [reverse cause / third factor]" (PT134-S3-Q6).
40	- **Each choice note runs the test its prefix calls for, and says so in the first line.** "Fails to consider / overlooks X" means ask whether X weakens. "Presumes / takes for granted X" means negate it and ask whether that weakens. "Concludes X on the grounds of Y" or "mistakes X for Y" means X must match the conclusion and Y the evidence (PT155-S1-Q20, PT148-S1-Q2). ===== PT146-S3-Q1 Flaw key A
-- A: This is the Sampling flaw answer we were looking for.
['It draws a conclusion about a population from observations of a subgroup that is quite likely to be unrepresentative of that population in certain relevant respects.']
## Evaluate
This is a very math-y argument, so the flaw is probably related to math. When we see arguments involving percentages, they often involve an illicit switch between percentages and numbers.
  For example, if an author saw that a certain company went from being 40% female to being 50% female, they would assume that there were more females than before. But just because a percentage went up doesn't mean the raw number went up. It could be like this:
  ```
  THEN       NOW
  4 women    4 women
  6 men      4 men
  40% women  50% women
  ```
  In this argument, Wilson went from being 50% of hairdryers sold to 25%. Is the author assuming that since the percentage went down, the raw number went down?
  Yes! And if the raw number did go down, then the conclusion is totally valid.
  If Wilson sold a smaller number of hairdryers last year, compared to five years ago, but they still make the exact same net income (i.e. profit) per hairdryer, then they would be making less net income from that product. Again, let's consider numbers.
  ```

**Handoff vs. wrapup:** run `session-handoff` when the *context window* is the problem — nearing ~250k tokens (the dumb zone), or passing work between Claude and Codex. It is chat-only and writes nothing. Run `wrapup` when the *work day* is done — it strikes tasks, refreshes `wiki/hot.md`, and appends `wiki/log.md`. They can be run back to back (wrapup to persist, then handoff to reset).

## When to invoke

Joshua says: "session handoff", "hand off", "handoff summary", "summarize before I clear", or any near-equivalent. Note "let's wrap up" belongs to `wrapup`, not here — if he says that and the context window is also deep, run `wrapup` first, then offer this. Also invoke proactively if he says he's about to `/clear` without having run it, or if the session is clearly deep into the dumb zone.

## How to produce the summary

1. **Review the full conversation**, not just the last few turns. Handoffs miss things when they only summarize recent context.
2. **Pull state from these sources (in order):**
   - Plan files referenced this session (check `~/.claude/plans/` if a plan was mentioned).
   - TodoWrite state — any in-progress or pending tasks.
   - Background processes started with `run_in_background` — shell IDs are load-bearing for the next agent.
   - Files created or modified this session — you know what you touched; don't grep to re-discover.
   - Memory files written or updated (`~/.claude/projects/C--Users-Joshu-dev-ai-os/memory/`).
   - Unresolved questions — things you asked Joshua that never got a clear answer, or things he asked that got deflected.
3. **Do NOT audit the filesystem.** This is synthesis of what happened in THIS session. No `git log`, no broad `Glob` sweeps. If you didn't touch it this session, it doesn't belong here.
4. **Produce the output in chat.** Do not write a file. Do not update memory. Chat-only.

## Output template — use exactly this structure, every time

```
# Session Handoff — <one-line title of what this session was about>

## Where it started
<2-3 sentences: what Joshua asked for, key framing or constraints that emerged>

## Decisions locked + what shipped
- <decision or change> — <why, and where it lives (absolute path if a file)>
- ...

## Key files for next session
- `<absolute path>` — <why the next agent should read this first>
- Plan file: `<path>` (if a plan drove the session)
- Memory files touched: `<paths>` (if any)

## Running state
- Background processes: <shell IDs + what they are + how to kill> — or "none"
- Dev servers / ports: <url + port> — or "none"
- Open worktrees / branches: <paths> — or "none"

## Verified state as of <HH:MM>
- <claim about live/system state> — <how it was checked, and when>
- <claim> — NOT re-verified this session; last confirmed <when>
- ...

## Verification — how to confirm things still work
- `<command>` — <expected outcome>
- ...

## Deferred + open questions
- Deferred: <item> — <why pushed to later>
- OPEN (must be resolved or re-asked before new work): <question needing Joshua's input> — <context>

## Pick up here
<1-2 sentences: the single most likely next action for a fresh agent>
```

## Hard rules

1. **Chat output only.** Never write the handoff to a file. Never update memory from this skill. (That is `wrapup`'s job, not this one.)
2. **Never invent state.** If a section has nothing to report, write "none" — do not omit the section. Structure stability is the whole point.
3. **Absolute paths always.** The next agent may have a different working directory, or be Codex.
4. **If a plan file drove the session, name it first** in "Key files" so the next agent reads it before anything else.
5. **No emojis, no hype, no "great job" summaries.** Terse and concrete — paths, commands, shell IDs, decisions. Tone of a seasoned engineer handing off at end-of-shift.
6. **Background process IDs are critical.** If you started any `run_in_background` shells, their IDs must appear in "Running state" with the kill command — the next agent cannot find them otherwise.
7. **Stamp verified state, and separate it from assumed state.** Run `date "+%H:%M"` and use the real time. Every claim about live systems (deploy status, DB contents, what was sent, what is published) is either something you actually checked this session — say how — or explicitly marked NOT re-verified. A handoff that presents stale belief as current state makes the next session re-derive everything, which is the exact cost this skill exists to remove.
8. **Open questions are obligations, not notes.** Anything under OPEN must be resolved by the next session or re-asked to Joshua before it starts new work. Requirements have been silently re-typed across sessions, and a promised artifact once never arrived because nobody re-asked. If a question was open in the handoff you are picking up from, it is the first thing you raise.

## Anti-patterns — do not do these

- Summarizing the last 3 turns and calling it a handoff.
- Listing files by relative path.
- Skipping "Running state" because "nothing is running" — write "none" instead.
- Writing the summary to any file. This is chat-only by design.
- Adding a "what went well / what went poorly" retrospective. This isn't a retro.
- Recommending next steps beyond the single "Pick up here" line. The next agent decides; you just hand off.
